item.title: Channel Managers for Hotels: The Complete 2026 Guide
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
You are losing 30 hours a week and thousands of euros a year. You may not know it, but if you still manage Booking.com, Airbnb, Expedia and the rest by hand, you are giving away revenue, time and — worse — your online reputation. Every overbooking costs an average of €1,200 once you add up refunds, relocation and bad reviews. And yet 67% of Italian properties under 100 rooms still work without a channel manager.

If you run a hotel, host a B&B or manage any kind of accommodation, this guide gives you what you need in 2026 to stop chasing the calendar and start earning more while working less.

What a channel manager is, in plain words

Imagine having ten assistants, one for each booking platform (Booking, Airbnb, Expedia, Agoda, Hotels.com and so on), and that the moment a room is booked on any one of them, all ten update their records instantly.

That is exactly what a channel manager is: software that synchronises in real time your availability, your rates and your bookings across every OTA (online travel agency) you are connected to. You work in a single dashboard; it talks to every channel on your behalf.

📌 In two lines: the channel manager is the technical bridge between your PMS (property management system) and every portal you sell on. Without it, each booking that arrives means manual updates on five to ten platforms.

Why hotels lose money without one

Let us talk about real figures, not theory. Here is what happens when everything is done by hand.

1. You lose 30 hours a week to repetitive work

A study by Hotrec (the European hospitality confederation) calculated that an average property spends between 20 and 35 hours a week on:

  • Updating availability by hand on every portal
  • Changing rates according to the season
  • Entering bookings into the PMS after receiving them by email
  • Answering messages on four or five different platforms

At a staff cost of €15 an hour, that is €23,400 a year burnt on work software can do on its own.

2. You suffer overbookings that cost an average of €1,200 each

When two guests book the same room on different portals within minutes of each other, and you have not updated availability in time, you are in overbooking. The average cost of each episode includes:

  • Full refund: €300–600
  • Relocation to a partner property, usually at a higher rate: €200–400
  • A penalty from the portal (Booking can charge up to 100% of the value): variable
  • A bad review, which on average costs you 9% of future revenue

3. You sell at the wrong price at exactly the wrong moment

Without synchronisation, a room is often still published at a low rate on Airbnb while you have already raised it on Booking. The result: you sell below price precisely when demand is highest.

How a channel manager works, technically

Here is the simplified flow, from the moment of booking to every channel being updated:

   ┌─────────────┐
   │    GUEST    │
   │   books on  │
   │   Booking   │
   └──────┬──────┘
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────────┐
   │ CHANNEL MANAGER │ ◄──── receives the booking via API
   │   (Dashboard)   │
   └──────┬──────────┘
          │
          ├──► Airbnb: closes availability
          ├──► Expedia: closes availability
          ├──► Agoda: closes availability
          ├──► Hotels.com: closes availability
          ├──► Your own website: updates the calendar
          │
          ▼
   ┌─────────────┐
   │     PMS     │ ◄──── booking recorded
   │             │
   └─────────────┘

All of this happens in under 30 seconds. You do nothing. You simply see the booking arrive in your system and the money in your account.

The platforms you need to be on

A modern channel manager should let you sell on at least these channels, chosen according to your market:

PlatformMarket share (Italy)Average commissionBest suited to
Booking.com~ 68%15–18%Hotels of any size, B&Bs
Airbnb~ 14%3–15%B&Bs, holiday homes, boutique hotels
Expedia / Hotels.com~ 9%15–20%3–5 star hotels, business travel
Agoda~ 4%15–18%Asian market, medium and large hotels
Despegar / Trip.com~ 3%15–20%Latin American and Asian markets
Your own site plus a booking engine~ 2%0–2%Everyone — this is your direct sale
💡 A strategic note: do not rely on Booking alone. Spreading across four or five channels reduces single-platform risk and lets you reach different segments — Airbnb brings more young travellers and families, Expedia more business trips.

How to choose the right one: seven criteria

The market offers dozens of options (SiteMinder, Cubilis, Octorate, RoomCloud, Smoobu, Lodgify, Beds24 and many more). To avoid a bad choice, weigh these seven:

CriterionWhat to checkWhy it matters
1. OTA connectivityHow many portals are integrated, and the quality of the connections (certified XML versus scraping)A poor connection means delays, and delays mean overbooking
2. PMS integrationDoes it talk to the system you already use?Without PMS integration you enter every booking twice
3. Booking engineDoes it include an engine for your own website?Direct sales mean no commission
4. Intelligent pricingDoes it allow automatic rules and dynamic pricing?Optimised rates mean 15–25% more RevPAR
5. ReportingClear dashboards, KPIs in real timeYou cannot improve what you do not measure
6. Support in your languageSeven-day support, ideally in your own time zoneWhen something breaks at 10pm on a Saturday you need a person
7. Transparent pricingCost per room per month, with no hidden commissionSome providers take a percentage of bookings: expensive over time

What it costs, and what it returns

The cost depends on the number of rooms and the modules you switch on. Typical ranges in 2026:

  • 1–10 rooms (B&Bs): €25–60 a month
  • 10–30 room hotels: €70–150 a month
  • 30–80 room hotels: €150–300 a month
  • 80+ rooms or groups: €300–800 a month

Working out the return: a real example

Take a 40-room hotel with an average rate of €95 a night and 65% occupancy:

ItemWithout a channel managerWith one
Software cost€0€180/month = €2,160/year
Hours spent on OTAs30h/week × €15 × 52 = €23,4005h/week × €15 × 52 = €3,900
Average overbookings per year8 × €1,200 = €9,6000–1 × €1,200 = €600
Rooms sold below price~ €7,000 in lost revenue~ €500
Higher occupancy (+8–12%)baseline+€18,000 extra revenue
Annual balance−€40,000 in losses and inefficiency+€34,840 net gain

In other words: for every €1 spent on a channel manager you recover 16 in efficiency and extra revenue.

A real case: an 80-room hotel on Ischia, before and after

A four-star hotel on Ischia, 80 rooms, open from March to November. Family-run, with two administrative staff. Starting point (2023):

  • Selling on Booking, Expedia and the website, all managed by hand
  • One person spending six hours a day on the portals alone
  • 12–15 overbookings during 2023, two of which meant relocating guests to a competitor at a higher rate
  • Review score: 8.1 on Booking, and falling
  • Static pricing: the same rate in August as in May

What we did in 60 days

  1. Audit: mapped every active channel and every manual step
  2. Chose the system: implemented Octorate with certified XML connections to all portals
  3. PMS integration: connected to the system already in place
  4. Added three new channels: Airbnb (families), Agoda (Asian market), Hotels.com
  5. Automatic rules: dynamic pricing based on occupancy, plus minimum-stay restrictions on high-season weekends
  6. Team training: eight hours on the new dashboard

Results after 12 months

Average occupancy62%74%+12%
Average daily rate (ADR)€105€124+18%
RevPAR€65€92+41%

Total season revenue€1,180,000€1,670,000+€490,000
"For the first month I was sceptical — I thought it was yet another piece of software that complicates your life. After three months I realised I had four more hours a day for the real work: talking to guests, looking after the property, training the team. The difference showed in that same season." — Manager, hotel on Ischia (80 rooms)

Implementing one in 30 days: the checklist

Week 1 — Audit and choice

  1. A complete list of the channels you currently sell on
  2. Check integration with your current PMS
  3. Set a monthly budget (see the price table above)
  4. Shortlist three candidates
  5. Take a free demo of each
  6. Choose your provider

Week 2 — Technical setup

  1. Create the account and configure the property (rooms, types, photos)
  2. Connect Booking.com (approval takes three to five days)
  3. Connect the other OTAs
  4. Integrate with your existing PMS
  5. Test synchronisation with a dummy booking

Week 3 — Pricing and rules

  1. Set base rates for each room type
  2. Configure dynamic pricing rules
  3. Set restrictions (minimum stay, closed to arrival)
  4. Test rate publication

Week 4 — Launch and training

  1. Train the operations team
  2. Go live
  3. Monitor daily for the first two weeks
  4. Tune against real data
  5. Establish weekly reporting
⚠️ One warning: do not underestimate the training. The most powerful channel manager in the world is useless if your team cannot use it. Allow at least eight hours spread over two or three sessions.

Related reading

If this was useful, read also:

  • How to avoid overbooking: a practical guide for hotels and B&Bs — a close look at problem number one for anyone running accommodation
  • Local SEO for hotels: reaching Google's top three in 90 days — why a channel manager without organic visibility is not enough

In closing: it is not a cost, it is a lever

If you run accommodation in 2026 and you still do not have a channel manager, you are leaving money on the table every single day. The question is not whether you need one, but how much you are losing until you have it.

The return is demonstrable, the technology is mature, and — most of all — your competitors are already using it. Every day you wait is a day of advantage you hand to the property next door.

item.title: How to Avoid Overbooking: A Practical Guide for Hotels and B&Bs
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
It is 11.40pm on a Saturday in July. A family of four arrives at your reception desk with their booking confirmation printed out. Smiling. Tired. Hungry. You check the system: you gave that room to another couple twenty minutes ago. Welcome to the worst nightmare in accommodation: overbooking.

It is not only embarrassing. Each episode costs an average of €1,200 and — worse — can damage your online reputation for months. The good news? In 95% of cases it is entirely avoidable, if you put the right measures in place.

What overbooking is, and why it really happens

Overbooking happens when you sell more rooms than you actually have for a given date. Technically it is simple; in practice it comes from four main causes:

  1. Slow synchronisation between portals — the booking arrives on Booking.com, but availability on Airbnb updates fifteen minutes later. In those fifteen minutes someone books the same room.
  2. Human error — a member of staff forgets to close availability on a channel after a phone booking.
  3. Deliberate overselling — some chains practise controlled overselling, counting on cancellations. A risky strategy for anyone without the experience to run it.
  4. Miscalculated no-show history — you overestimate how many guests will not turn up and accept more bookings than you should.
⚠️ A myth worth killing: "overbooking only happens to large properties". It does not. Four-room B&Bs have proportionally the same overbooking rate as hundred-room hotels, because they often run less sophisticated systems.

What a single overbooking really costs

When it happens, you do not only pay the visible damage. Here is the real breakdown of a typical episode, based on a double room at €130 a night:

Cost itemAverage amountNotes
Refund to the guest€130Returning the rate paid
Relocation to a partner hotel€180–250Often at a higher rate than yours
Transport for the guest (taxi)€20–40Not optional, in practice
OTA penalty, where applied€0–200Booking can suspend your account
Voucher or future discount as an apology€50–100To keep the guest
Bad review (average impact)~€6009% of lost future revenue over six months
Estimated total€1,150–1,350For a single room

And if the episode goes viral — TripAdvisor, travel groups on Facebook, Reddit — the damage grows fast. A hotel in Sorrento calculated losses of €18,000 in 2024 after an overbooking ended up in a Reddit thread with 40,000 views.

The seven mistakes that cause overbooking

Mistake 1: relying on manual updates

You tell yourself you check every morning. But overbooking arrives at 11pm on a Saturday, not at 9am on a Monday.

Mistake 2: a channel manager without certified XML

Some cheap channel managers use scraping instead of official XML connections. The result: delays of five to fifteen minutes on every update.

Mistake 3: selling on too many channels without control

More portals means more potential sources of overbooking if synchronisation is not perfect. Five well-synced channels beat twelve half-connected ones.

Mistake 4: not protecting your scarce rooms

Suites, junior suites, accessible rooms — the ones you only have one or two of — deserve special rules: a two-night minimum, no last-minute sales.

Mistake 5: ignoring seasonality

In high season the risk is four times higher. It calls for stricter rules.

Mistake 6: a PMS disconnected from the channel manager

If a direct booking from your website does not automatically update OTA availability, you are exposed.

Mistake 7: never reading the synchronisation logs

Channel managers record every update. If you never look at them, you will not know when something goes wrong.

Fix 1: a channel manager with real-time sync

This is the foundation. Without a modern channel manager with certified XML connections, every other measure limps.

The technical essentials:

  • Push notifications from the portals, so bookings arrive in milliseconds, not minutes
  • Certified XML connections (not scraping) for Booking.com, Expedia, Airbnb and Agoda
  • Two-way API with your PMS
  • Synchronisation logs you can read in real time
  • Automatic alerts when something looks wrong
📊 A figure: properties moving from manual management to a certified channel manager cut overbooking episodes by 92% in the first year (source: Hotelmize, 2024).

Fix 2: a deliberate safety buffer

Even with the best channel manager there is always a theoretical margin of risk — two bookings in the same fraction of a second. The answer is a buffer: keep one or two rooms off the portals during critical periods.

How to size it

Property sizeLow seasonHigh seasonEvents and peaks
Up to 10 rooms01 room1 room
10–30 rooms0–11–2 rooms2 rooms
30–80 rooms12–3 rooms3–4 rooms
80+ rooms1–23–5 rooms4–6 rooms

The buffer is not lost revenue: it is insurance. Whatever is left you sell at the last minute directly, or you use it to absorb any overbooking that still slips through.

Fix 3: automatic stop-sell rules

Configure your channel manager to close sales automatically when certain conditions are met:

  • When two or fewer rooms of a type remain, raise the rate by 25%
  • When one room of a type remains, close every channel except your own site
  • On high-risk dates — events, long weekends, summer Saturdays — set a two or three night minimum stay
  • Block same-day bookings after 10pm on the portals with the slowest sync
💡 A professional's trick: at demand peaks (New Year, mid-August, Easter), close the last two or three rooms on every portal 48 hours ahead and handle them only from reception or by phone. You cut the overbooking risk by 90% and still sell at your top rate.

🛡️ Want to take overbooking to zero?

Request a free audit 📱 Talk to us on WhatsApp

A real case: a 12-room B&B in Posillipo

A twelve-room B&B in Naples (Posillipo), family-run, selling on Booking, Airbnb, Expedia and its own site.

Starting point (2023)

  • Running on a cheap channel manager based on scraping
  • Nine overbookings during the year, four of them in July and August
  • Estimated total cost: €11,700 across refunds, relocations and revenue lost to bad reviews
  • Booking score down from 9.1 to 8.5 in eight months

What we changed

  1. Replaced the cheap system with an enterprise one using certified XML — cost: €60 more a month
  2. Introduced a one-room buffer in August, none in low season
  3. Stop-sell rules: close the OTA channels when one room remains
  4. Two-night minimum stay on July and August weekends
  5. An SMS alert to the owner for any booking that leaves fewer than two rooms free

Results over the following 12 months

KPI20232024
Overbooking episodes90
Cost of overbooking€11,700€0
Average room rate€95€114 (+20%)
Booking score8.59.2
Return on the new channel manager—16×
"I thought spending €60 more a month was a waste. I changed my mind on the first of August: no stress, no angry guests, and with the minimum stay I raised my rates too. It paid for itself in three weeks." — Owner, B&B in Posillipo

A ten-point anti-overbooking checklist

Print it, pin it up in the office, go through it once a month:

  1. ✅ I have a channel manager with certified XML on every main channel
  2. ✅ My PMS has a two-way integration with it
  3. ✅ I have a safety buffer set for my peak season
  4. ✅ I have automatic stop-sell rules for scarce room types
  5. ✅ I have minimum-stay rules for critical periods
  6. ✅ I receive automatic alerts for synchronisation anomalies
  7. ✅ I read the sync logs at least once a week
  8. ✅ My team knows what to do when an overbooking happens — a written protocol
  9. ✅ I have relocation agreements with at least two partner hotels of the same standard
  10. ✅ I review every episode, even small ones, to understand the cause and prevent the next

What to do when it happens anyway

Even with every precaution it can still happen. Here is the emergency protocol:

  1. Tell the guest immediately — do not wait for check-in
  2. Apologise plainly and take responsibility
  3. Offer relocation to a property of higher standard, never lower
  4. Cover the transport and the price difference
  5. Add a voucher or discount for a future stay
  6. Follow up the next day with a personal phone call
  7. Ask for private feedback before the public review

Handled well, the emergency can turn a bad episode into a neutral or even positive review. Eight guests in ten who are looked after properly after an overbooking do not leave a negative review.

In closing: overbooking is prevented, not managed

Every euro spent on prevention — channel manager, automatic rules, training — saves you at least €10–15 in direct and indirect costs. The question is not whether to invest, but how quickly.

If you have had even one overbooking in the past twelve months, it is time to act. Waiting only means adding another €1,200 of losses each time it happens.

item.title: Local SEO for Hotels: Reaching Google's Top Three in 90 Days
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
"Hotels in Naples historic centre". You type it into Google. Three properties appear in the local pack — the map with the top three results. The other 47 properties in the area? Invisible. Seventy-six per cent of people never scroll past those first three local results. If you are not there, you do not exist.

The good news: reaching Google's top three for local searches is a science, not an art. It is called local SEO, and with 90 days of structured work you can go from invisible to first in your area. Here is how.

Why local SEO is a different game

Classic SEO optimises your site for global rankings ("best carbonara recipe"). Local SEO optimises for searches with geographic intent ("hotel Naples centre", "restaurant Sorrento near the sea").

Google uses different algorithms for the two. For local searches it weighs three main factors:

FactorWeight in the algorithmWhat it means
Relevance~ 30%Does your Google Business Profile actually answer what the person is looking for?
Proximity~ 40%How close are you to the place searched for, or to the person searching?
Prominence~ 30%How well known you are online: reviews, links, mentions, citations

You have little control over the first two — your building is where it is. But prominence is built, and that is where the game is won.

📌 A key figure: 46% of all Google searches have local intent. In tourism that rises to 78%. In other words: eight searches in ten in this sector are local SEO opportunities.

Google Business Profile: ten points to optimise

Your Google Business Profile (formerly Google My Business) is the heart of local SEO. Getting it right is worth more than months of work on the website. Here is the full checklist.

1. Primary and secondary categories

Get the primary category exactly right ("Hotel", not "Lodging"). Add two to four relevant secondary categories ("Bed & breakfast", "3-star hotel", "Boutique hotel").

2. Consistent name, address and phone (NAP)

Your NAP must be identical everywhere online — website, social, directories, OTAs. Even "Street" versus "St." can confuse Google.

3. Photos: at least 30, properly taken

  • Exterior: façade, sign, entrance
  • Rooms: every type, at least three angles
  • Shared areas: lobby, restaurant, pool, terrace
  • Bathrooms: the details, shower, bath
  • Team: staff at work — it makes the brand human
  • Views: what guests actually see from the rooms

4. An optimised description

750 characters. Put your main keyword ("hotel Naples centre") in the first 250. Mention two or three selling points: "five minutes from the cathedral", "breakfast included", "private parking".

5. Every attribute filled in

Complete all the available attributes: free Wi-Fi, pets allowed, accessibility, payment methods, family facilities and so on. More attributes means more matches with specific searches.

6. Weekly posts

Publish one post a week: offers, events, news from the property. Google rewards active profiles in local ranking.

7. Questions and answers, looked after

Public questions should be answered within 24 hours. Add the most frequent ones yourself, with well-written answers.

8. Reviews: plenty of them, properly handled

See the dedicated section below. Reviews are the single biggest prominence factor.

9. Products and services

Create an entry for each room type, special package and service — transfers, excursions, restaurant. Each one is an extra page of local SEO.

10. Direct messaging switched on

Let people write to you straight from Google. Answer within an hour, or Google penalises the profile.

Local keywords: how to find them for free

Do not chase generic terms like "hotels in Italy". Go for local long-tail phrases: more specific, less competitive.

Free tools that actually work

  1. Google Suggest — start typing "hotel naples" and read the autocomplete
  2. People Also Ask in the Google results page
  3. AnswerThePublic (free tier) — shows every related question
  4. Google Trends — compare volumes and seasonality
  5. Keyword Surfer (free Chrome extension)

Examples of high-intent local keywords

KeywordMonthly volume (Italy)DifficultyIntent
hotel naples historic centre~ 8,100HighDirect booking
hotel naples near the station~ 2,400MediumDirect booking
cheap B&B naples with breakfast~ 880LowDirect booking
hotel naples with parking~ 1,300MediumDirect booking
hotel naples sea view~ 720Medium-lowDirect booking
where to stay near naples cathedral~ 320LowResearch and booking

The winning approach: two or three head keywords with high volume, and 15 to 20 long-tail ones, each with its own page or section.

On-page SEO for hotels: the technical pieces

Title tag

Hotel Naples Historic Centre | [Hotel Name] — 4 Stars, 100m from the Cathedral

Sixty characters at most, main keyword at the start, selling point at the end.

Meta description

155 characters at most, keyword plus a call to action: "Four-star hotel in the heart of Naples, 100m from the cathedral. Free Wi-Fi, breakfast included. Book now for our best rate."

Hotel schema markup (JSON-LD)

Implement Schema.org's Hotel type on your site. It lets Google read your stars, prices, reviews and GPS location. Properties with complete schema markup see 32% more clicks from search results.

Structured URLs

  • yourhotel.com/rooms/double-room-sea-view ✅
  • yourhotel.com/?page=125&room=003 ❌

Heading hierarchy

One H1 per page, H2 for main sections, H3 for sub-sections. Main keyword in the H1, variations in the H2s.

💡 An advanced trick: build "location" pages for the landmarks near your hotel ("Hotels near Castel Nuovo", "Where to stay near Spaccanapoli"). They rank easily because no competitor bothers to make them.

Local link building that works

Links from relevant sites are still an important ranking factor. In tourism, aim for:

  1. Local tourism directories — the city council site, regional tourist boards
  2. Partnerships with attractions — "partner hotel of the archaeological museum", with a reciprocal link
  3. Travel bloggers — a complimentary stay in exchange for an article (mind the disclosure rules: it must be declared)
  4. Local press releases — when something is new, send it to the local papers
  5. Events and sponsorships — sponsoring a cultural event earns a link from the event site
  6. Universities and colleges — work with tourism and hospitality courses; academic links carry weight
⚠️ Never do this: buying links, mass link exchanges, generic low-quality directories. Google penalises them heavily. Five good links beat 500 toxic ones.

Reviews: how to get more of them, legitimately

Google reviews are the single biggest prominence factor. Properties with 50 or more reviews and an average above 4.5 appear in the local pack three times as often as those with fewer.

A system that keeps producing reviews

  1. A QR code in the room that goes straight to your Google review page
  2. An automatic email 24 hours after check-out with a short link
  3. Asking in person at check-out: "If your stay was a good one, a Google review would help us enormously"
  4. A WhatsApp follow-up two days after they get home
  5. Never a cash incentive — Google forbids it. You may offer "10% off your next stay" as a general thank-you, not tied to leaving a review

How to reply

  • To every one, within 48 hours — the good ones included
  • Work local keywords into your replies ("Thank you for choosing our hotel in the heart of Naples…")
  • For negative reviews: apologise, offer a fix, move to a private channel. Never argue in public

The checklist: 30 steps over 90 days

Weeks 1–2: foundations

  1. Audit the current Google Business Profile
  2. Check NAP consistency across the 20 main directories

Weeks 11–13: reviews and refinement

  1. Automatic review request system

In closing: local SEO is not optional

In 2026, if you run accommodation and you are not in Google's local pack for your main keywords, you are handing guests to your competitors. Every day. Literally.

item.title: From 5 to 20 Bookings a Month: A Naples Tour Agency Case Study
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
October 2023. A tour agency in Naples calls Experiences Srl. On the other end is Luca, the owner, sounding tired: "We get five bookings a month. All of them word of mouth. On Google we do not exist. I have run out of ideas."

Ten months later the same agency closes 2024 at 20 bookings a month on average, peaking at 35 in summer. Without hiring anyone. Without pouring money into advertising. Simply by digitising what they already did well, but invisibly.

This is the story — a real one, in detail, with figures — of how they got there. If you run a small agency, work as a self-employed guide or are building a tour operation, read to the end. Most of it transfers.

Where they started

The agency (we will call it "TourNap" for discretion) had been trading since 2019. It specialised in walking tours of the historic centre, excursions to the Royal Palace of Caserta and boat trips to Capri. Three partners, all with a decade of experience as guides.

Baseline figures (January–September 2023)

KPIValue
Average bookings per month5
Average order value€85 (individual) / €240 (group)
Average monthly revenue~€1,800
Where bookings came from90% word of mouth, 10% organic Facebook
WebsiteYes, but dating from 2019, not mobile-friendly, no booking
Presence on tour OTAsTripAdvisor only, and the profile was not optimised
Google position for "tours Naples"Page 4
Hours a week spent selling~3h (Facebook plus phone)

The problem was not the quality of the product — TourNap had excellent reviews from everyone who had tried it. The problem was that nobody could find them. Growth was stuck on a floor of word of mouth they could not climb off.

📌 The real problem: 73% of international travellers book tours online, before they travel. If you are not on the right channels, you simply do not exist for them.

What finally convinced them

They had resisted "going digital" for months. Three familiar objections:

  1. "We have no marketing budget"
  2. "The platforms take too much commission"
  3. "Word of mouth still works, why change?"

The turning point came when they discovered that a direct competitor — founded after them, with less experienced guides — was turning over eight times as much. The secret? They were everywhere online.

They called Experiences Srl for a free audit. After 90 minutes of analysis the plan was clear. They said yes.

Step 1: a mobile-first website (days 1–21)

The existing site was a 2019 brochure: slow, not responsive, no booking system, poor photography. We rewrote it from scratch around these priorities.

What the new site had

  • Mobile-first: 78% of tourism traffic comes from phones
  • Under two seconds to load, with Core Web Vitals in the green
  • Bilingual Italian and English from the start, with room for German and French later
  • A built-in booking engine with online payment (Stripe and PayPal)
  • A page for each tour with professional photos, a map, FAQs and embedded reviews
  • An AI chatbot answering around the clock in three languages
  • Tour schema markup for search

Before and after, in raw site numbers

MetricOld siteNew site
Mobile load time6.8s1.4s
Mobile usability score52/10098/100
Visitor-to-booking conversion0.4%3.2%
Bounce rate78%34%
LanguagesItalian onlyItalian and English

Step 2: getting onto the tour platforms (days 15–40)

Alongside the site, we connected TourNap to the main OTAs in the tours sector. Spreading across channels was essential to get off word of mouth.

The platforms we activated

PlatformCommissionMain audienceTime to go live
GetYourGuide20–30%International travellers, mobile4 weeks
Viator (TripAdvisor)25%American and English-speaking3 weeks
Airbnb Experiences20%Younger travellers, authentic experiences6 weeks (selection process)
Musement20–25%European, culture-led2 weeks
Klook20%Asian market3 weeks

Yes, the commissions are high. But this is volume you would never see without the platforms. And with booking on your own site at zero commission, the mix balances out. The rule: aim to make your own site at least 30% of sales.

Optimising the platform listings

Signing up is not enough. Each tour listing on an OTA is a small SEO page in its own right. For every tour:

  • A title built around the main keywords
  • A description of 1,500–2,000 characters, structured in points
  • Ten to fifteen high-resolution professional photographs
  • A detailed itinerary with timings
  • Highlights as a list — what makes this tour different
  • FAQs written around what people actually search for
  • Clear policies: cancellation, meeting point, accessibility

Step 3: local SEO for tours in Naples (days 30–90)

The platforms bring traffic, but Google is still the first door. Working on local SEO for tour keywords changed the picture.

Target keywords

KeywordMonthly volumeStarting positionPosition at 90 days
tour naples historic centre3,600—4
walking tour naples1,300—2
half day excursions naples720—1
caserta palace tour from naples880—3
walking tour Naples Italy2,100—5

What the SEO work involved

  1. Google Business Profile completed to 100%, with more than 50 photographs
  2. A dedicated page for each tour — eight pages, each over 1,500 words
  3. Six blog articles in the first 90 days ("What to see in Naples in two days", "Ten hidden corners of the historic centre" and so on)
  4. TouristAttraction and Event schema markup
  5. Link building: twelve links from travel blogs and local sites
  6. An automatic system asking for Google reviews after each tour

🚀 Want to grow the way TourNap did?

Experiences Srl has taken dozens of agencies and tour operators to three to five times their bookings in 90 to 180 days. Modern site, OTA integration, SEO, AI chatbot — handled end to end.

Request a free consultation 📱 WhatsApp us

Step 4: an AI chatbot for round-the-clock bookings (days 60–75)

Forty-one per cent of enquiries arrived outside office hours. In plain terms: they were losing potential bookings every evening, every night, every weekend.

We put a multilingual AI chatbot on the site and on WhatsApp Business, able to:

  • Answer in Italian, English and Spanish
  • Know every tour, its price, its times and its meeting point
  • Handle the FAQs: cancellation policy, accessibility, children, the language of the tour
  • Check availability in real time
  • Take the visitor all the way to a completed booking
  • Hand over to the owner on WhatsApp only when a request is genuinely complex

What the chatbot did in its first 60 days

  • 340 conversations handled
  • 187 enquiries resolved on their own
  • 47 bookings generated
  • 92% satisfaction after the conversation
  • Average response time: 2 seconds, against six hours before
💡 The telling detail: 31% of the bookings the chatbot generated arrive between 9pm and 2am. That night window is mostly American and Asian travellers planning from home.

Results at 30, 60 and 90 days

Here is what actually happened, month by month, in the first 90 days after the new setup went live:

Total bookings per month581319
Bookings from the own site0357

Airbnb Experiences bookings0012

Monthly revenue€1,800€2,900€4,800€7,100

Twelve months on (January 2025)

KPI2023 (before)2024 (after)
Total bookings per year~60~240
Average bookings per month520
Summer peak (one month)935
Average order value€85€97 (+14%)
Annual revenue~€21,000~€92,000
Direct sales share (own site)0%38%
Google reviews18 (4.7)147 (4.8)
Position for "tours Naples"Page 4Position 4 (page 1)
"I was sceptical at first. I thought spending on a website and marketing would just burn resources. Six months later I had changed my mind. The most important thing? We do not work more: we work better. The platforms and the chatbot do the heavy lifting. We guide, which is what we actually love." — Luca, owner of TourNap

What you can do too: the checklist

There is nothing magic in TourNap's path. Any small agency or tour operator can repeat it. Here it is in eight points.

  1. Audit where you are now. What do you turn over? Where do guests come from? What is your conversion rate? Without a baseline you cannot tell whether anything is working.
  2. A mobile-first site with booking built in. This is not optional. Without it you lose seven visitors in ten. Typical one-off investment: €3,500–6,000.
  3. Go live on three to five tour OTAs. Start with GetYourGuide and Viator. Add Airbnb Experiences and Musement in the following months.
  4. Structured local SEO. Google Business Profile, content, schema markup. See the dedicated guide.
  5. An AI chatbot for round-the-clock enquiries. Especially if your market is international. Cost: €80–200 a month, with an excellent return.
  6. An automatic review system. Email or WhatsApp after the tour, with a direct link. Target: at least five to ten new reviews a month.
  7. A channel manager for tours. Once you pass 50 bookings a month across several platforms you need one. See the channel manager guide for tour operators.
  8. Monthly analysis. Measure everything. What works? What does not? Adjust as you go, not at year end.
⚠️ A common mistake: "I will do the website first, then think about the rest." Wrong. All eight should start in parallel during the first 60 to 90 days. Waiting to perfect one thing before beginning the next slows everything down.

In closing: digital does not replace, it amplifies

TourNap already had everything: passion, expertise, quality. What was missing was the amplifier that would let the world hear about it. Digital does not make you good if you are not: it makes you findable if you already are.

If you run a small agency or tour operation and you recognise yourself in TourNap's starting point, the path is clear, tested and repeatable. You do not have to be big to reach good numbers. You have to be present in the right places.

item.title: GetYourGuide vs Viator vs Your Own Site: Where to Sell Your Tours in 2026
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
The online tours market is worth $254 billion globally, and in Italy it grows 18% a year. Yet most guides and small agencies are still stuck on the same question: "Which platform should I sell my tours on?"

The right answer is not "one", but "the right mix for your case". GetYourGuide brings international volume. Viator dominates the English-speaking market. Airbnb Experiences suits certain audiences perfectly. Your own site pays no commission. But which combination works for you?

This guide compares the four main channels with real figures and real commissions, and helps you build the most profitable multi-channel strategy for your business in 2026.

The online tours market in 2026

Understanding the context matters before choosing where to sell. Here is where the market stands:

IndicatorGloballyItaly
Online tours and activities market$254bn~€8.1bn
Annual growth (CAGR 2023–2027)+11%+18%
Share of tours booked online74%67%
Share booked on mobile62%71%
Average booking lead time11 days8 days
OTA share of online bookings~58%~64%

In plain terms: if you sell tours and you are not on the main platforms, you lose access to 67% of the Italian market and 74% of the international one. Your own site alone is not enough — your customers look on the OTAs too.

GetYourGuide: strengths, weaknesses, commission

GetYourGuide is Europe's leading platform for tours and experiences. Founded in Germany in 2009, it now handles over 60,000 activities in 170 countries and 75 million bookings a year.

How it works

  1. You register as a supplier (verification and onboarding take two to four weeks)
  2. You build your tour listings following their guidelines, which are strict
  3. You set availability, prices and restrictions
  4. GetYourGuide brings customers, handles payments and support
  5. You run the tour and are paid monthly

Commission and costs

  • Standard: 20–25% of bookings
  • "Originals" (premium): 30%, but with more visibility and marketing
  • No fixed monthly fee
  • Payment at 60 days net

Strengths ✅

  • A high-quality international audience (Europe, USA, UK)
  • Invests heavily in SEO and advertising, which brings you traffic
  • A very strong mobile app — 60% of bookings
  • Dedicated support, with a real account manager
  • A rigorous review system, which raises the bar for your tours
  • Assisted dynamic pricing

Weaknesses ❌

  • High commission (20–30%)
  • Long, selective onboarding — they turn down 40% of applications
  • Strict quality standards for photos, descriptions and operations
  • Heavy dependency: if they drop you, you lose a key channel
  • Low visibility for new tours until the first reviews arrive
📌 When GetYourGuide is the right fit: you are a guide or agency with genuinely high quality, you want access to the international market, and you have time to do the onboarding properly.

Viator (TripAdvisor Experiences)

Viator is the TripAdvisor group's tours platform: over 300,000 experiences across 1,500 destinations, strongest in English-speaking markets — the USA, UK and Australia.

How it works

  1. Sign up through Viator Supplier — faster than GetYourGuide, one to two weeks
  2. Your listings are synced automatically with TripAdvisor
  3. The same logic applies for availability, pricing and bookings

Commission and costs

  • Standard: 25% of bookings
  • Payment: after the tour runs, on a 7–14 day cycle
  • No fixed fee

Strengths ✅

  • Two channels in one: Viator plus TripAdvisor from a single profile
  • A strong English-speaking audience (USA, Canada, UK, Australia)
  • Simpler onboarding than GetYourGuide
  • Good presence in mainstream markets
  • Automatic syncing of TripAdvisor reviews

Weaknesses ❌

  • High commission (25%)
  • Very strong internal competition — many similar tours
  • An opaque algorithm: it is hard to tell why some tours rank better than others
  • Support in English, with limited Italian
  • A less modern interface than GetYourGuide
📌 When Viator is the right fit: your tours appeal to an American or English-speaking audience, you already have good TripAdvisor reviews, and you want an additional channel with quicker onboarding.

Airbnb Experiences: who it suits

Airbnb Experiences is Airbnb's experiences arm. More selective, focused on authentic, local activities rather than tourism in the classic sense.

How it works

  1. You apply through Airbnb — a competitive process; roughly 15% of applicants are accepted
  2. A quality check by video call
  3. The experience has to be genuinely distinctive and rooted in the place
  4. Publishing and management happen through the Airbnb app

Commission and costs

  • Standard: 20% commission
  • No fixed fee
  • Payment after the experience runs

Strengths ✅

  • The lowest commission of the tour OTAs
  • A young audience (25–40) that is willing to spend
  • Fits the Airbnb context — the trip is already booked
  • "Local" experiences carry enormous perceived value
  • An excellent app and a very good booking experience

Weaknesses ❌

  • Highly selective onboarding, with a high rejection rate
  • Not suited to mainstream tours — coaches, classic group outings
  • Lower volume than GetYourGuide or Viator
  • Hard to scale beyond a certain size
  • The discovery algorithm does not always favour newcomers
📌 When Airbnb Experiences is the right fit: you are a guide with something genuinely personal — a cooking workshop, a street-art tour with a local artist, a craft experience. It is not the channel for a generic historic-centre walk.

Your own site: when it makes sense, and what it costs

Your own site with a booking engine is the most underrated and most profitable channel. No commission. Your customer. Your data. Your brand.

How it works

  1. Build a mobile-first site with a booking engine
  2. Integrate a payment gateway (Stripe, PayPal, Nexi)
  3. SEO-optimised pages for every tour
  4. An availability system, which can connect to a channel manager
  5. Direct marketing: SEO, social, email, advertising

Typical costs

  • Initial setup: €3,500–8,000 for a site plus a professional booking engine
  • Running costs: €40–150 a month for hosting, booking engine and plugins
  • Payment fees: 1.5–2.5% with Stripe or PayPal
  • Marketing: variable — SEO investment, optional advertising

Strengths ✅

  • No OTA commission
  • The customer is yours: email, data, the ability to market to them again
  • Free pricing, your own rules
  • Cross-selling and upselling — tour plus transfer plus lunch
  • Brand building that compounds
  • No dependence on someone else's algorithm

Weaknesses ❌

  • You have to bring the traffic yourself: SEO, social, advertising
  • A meaningful upfront investment
  • SEO results take six to twelve months
  • You handle payments, customer service and disputes
  • International travellers will not stumble across you

The winning approach: multi-channel

The right answer to "where should I sell?" is: do not pick one. Mix them deliberately.

FeatureGetYourGuideViatorAirbnb Exp.Own site
Commission20–30%25%20%0% (+2% payment fees)
Main audienceEurope, USAUSA, UKYoung, urbanAnyone looking for you
Potential volume★★★★★★★★★★★★★★ (grows over time)
Ease of entry★★★★★★★★★★★ (needs setup)
Brand building★★★★★★★★★★★★
Control of the customer★★★★★★★★★
Payment60 days net7–14 days24h after the tourImmediate

The mix to aim for, by stage

StageRecommended channelsTarget share from each
Starting out (0–50 bookings/month)GetYourGuide + Viator + a basic site45% / 35% / 20%
Growing (50–150/month)GetYourGuide + Viator + Airbnb Exp. + an optimised site35% / 25% / 15% / 25%

The key point: your own site grows over time. At the starting stage it is 20%; once established it passes 40%. That is the slice of revenue that pays no commission at all.

🎯 A multi-channel setup, ready in 60 days

Running several channels without losing your mind

If you sell on four or five channels at once, managing availability by hand is impossible and will sooner or later give you an overbooking or a pricing conflict.

The answer is a channel manager built for tours, which is a different thing from a hotel one. The main options in 2026:

  • Rezdy — widely used globally, good for mid-sized operators

120 tours, 8 selling platforms, 3 languages, 5 destinations. A tour operator in Naples showed us how they worked: four full-time people updating availability and prices by hand. Hours thrown away. Pricing errors on 12% of listings. Inventory out of sync. A team at its limit.

Sixty days after putting in a channel manager built for their sector: two people handled the same volume in an hour a day, pricing errors fell to 1%, and revenue grew 27% thanks to automatic dynamic pricing.

If you run a tour operation with more than 30 active tours across three or more platforms, this guide is for you. A channel manager for tour operators is not a nice-to-have: it is the difference between scaling and drowning.

Tour operators and hotels need different tools

Hotel channel managers (see the dedicated guide) manage rooms as static units. Tour operator systems have to handle something far more complicated: experiences with moving parts.

VariableHotel (traditional CM)Tour operator (dedicated CM)
Unit being managedRooms, a fixed numberSeats per tour × time slot × day
Time dimensionThe night, fixedSeveral slots within a day
PricingPer nightPer person, per ticket type, per time slot
Pricing variablesSeason, occupancySeason, language, group size, extras
CancellationsStandardSeveral policies per tour and per time window
Main OTAsBooking, Expedia, AirbnbGetYourGuide, Viator, Airbnb Exp., Musement, Klook
External dependenciesNoneVehicles, boats, museum tickets, guides

Using a hotel channel manager for a tour business is like doing advanced maths on a pocket calculator: fine for simple sums, but it falls apart as soon as things get complicated.

What actually goes wrong without one

1. Duplicated, out-of-sync inventory

The same 9am slot shows as available on GetYourGuide, Viator, Airbnb and your own site. Two bookings arrive in the same minute on different channels. Overbooking. You have to cancel a customer who has already paid.

2. Inconsistent pricing

You raised the "Pompeii half day" tour from €45 to €52 on GetYourGuide. On Viator it is still €45. On Airbnb it is €40. Three prices for the same tour means confused customers, bad reviews and lost margin.

3. An overloaded team

Your people spend 70% of their time on data entry instead of selling, building relationships and improving the experiences. Burnout within six months, dependably.

4. No room to grow

You would like to add 20 tours. You would like to enter the US and German markets. You would like to launch a new destination. But you cannot: the current setup would collapse.

5. No usable analytics

Which tour has the best margin? Which OTA brings the highest-spending customers? What is the conversion rate on each channel? You do not know. You decide blind.

⚠️ A warning sign: if you have more than 30 active tours and still manage availability in shared spreadsheets or over WhatsApp between staff, you are already in dangerous territory. It is only a matter of time before the first big, public overbooking.

What a tour operator channel manager needs in 2026

1. Multi-level inventory management

The system has to handle hierarchical inventory:

  • Physical resources: one coach is 50 seats, one boat is 12
  • People: which guides are available, for which slot and which language
  • External resources: museum tickets, pre-booked entries
  • Restrictions: minimum and maximum participants, age, language

2. Automatic dynamic pricing

Rules that change the price according to:

  • How far ahead of the tour date the booking is
  • How full the slot already is
  • The season
  • Local events and holidays
  • Historical demand, with machine learning

3. Two-way APIs with every OTA

Native, certified connections — not scraping — with:

  • GetYourGuide (official API)
  • Viator (Bókun API)
  • Airbnb Experiences (selective)
  • Musement
  • Klook
  • Civitatis
  • Headout
  • Tiqets

4. A booking engine for your own site

The system should include or integrate with a proper booking engine for your site, offering:

  • Multiple languages and currencies
  • Online payment (Stripe, PayPal, Klarna)
  • A mobile-first experience
  • Automatic cross-selling

5. Operations

  • Automatic manifests for guides, with the participant list
  • Automatic pre-tour messages to customers
  • Cancellations and refunds with differentiated rules
  • Mobile check-in lists

6. Reporting and business intelligence

  • Margin by tour, by OTA, by season
  • Conversion rate per channel
  • Customer lifetime value by source
  • Demand forecasting

💡 Worth knowing: Bókun, owned by TripAdvisor, is the native channel manager for Viator and is free for anyone selling there. An excellent entry point for a growing operator — you only pay once you take direct bookings or bookings from other OTAs.

Dynamic pricing for tours, and what it returns

Dynamic pricing means changing the price automatically according to demand, lead time and occupancy. For tours it works even better than for hotels, because there are more moving variables.

A real example: the Pompeii half-day tour

21 days out, 60% full€48€48 (standard)
7 days out, 85% full€48€56 (+17%, scarcity)
2 days out, 95% full€48€64 (+33%, last seats)
Same day, one seat left€48€72 (+50%, impulse)

Industry research shows dynamic pricing produces on average 15–25% more RevPAX (revenue per available passenger) than static pricing, without reducing volume.

The five layers of dynamic pricing

  1. Seasonal (the base): different prices for high, mid and low season
  2. Weekend against weekday: a premium on Saturdays and Sundays
  3. Events: a premium for holidays, long weekends and local events
  4. Lead time: early bird, standard, last minute
  5. Occupancy: automatic increases as thresholds are reached

Modern systems let you stack all five at once, with rules that combine automatically.

Implementing one: a 60-day roadmap

Weeks 1–2: audit and selection

  1. Map every tour, channel and workflow you have today
  2. Identify the weak points: errors, waste, risk
  3. Define must-haves and nice-to-haves
  4. Shortlist three or four candidates
  5. Demos and a proof of concept

Weeks 3–4: catalogue setup

  1. Migrate tours into a single consistent structure
  2. Configure resources: vehicles, people, external bookings
  3. Ticket types and variant pricing
  4. Differentiated cancellation policies
  5. Photos, descriptions and content in every language

Weeks 5–6: integrations

  1. Connect every OTA you are already on
  2. Add one or two strategically useful new ones
  3. Integrate your own site and payments
  4. Test bookings and cancellations across channels

Weeks 7–8: operations and launch

  1. Dynamic pricing on your top tours
  2. Manifests, customer messaging, check-in
  3. Team training, eight to sixteen hours
  4. Soft launch with close monitoring
  5. Continuous tuning on the first real data
📌 One piece of advice: do not wait for low season to make the switch. The truth is that there is no perfect moment. Do it as soon as you can — every month of delay is money left on the table.

In closing: scaling needs the right stack

If you run a tour operation with 30 or more active tours and you recognise the problems described here — inconsistent pricing, an overloaded team, sync errors, no room to grow — the solution exists, it is mature, and your competitors are already adopting it.

A channel manager is not a cost: it is the infrastructure that takes you from craft operation to a business that can scale. The typical return, as in the case above, is between fifteen and forty times in the first year.

item.title: AI Chatbots for Hotels and B&Bs: The Digital Front Desk That Works 24/7

Eighty-three per cent of the enquiries your property receives arrive outside working hours. You are asleep, at dinner, or in a room with a guest. And while you are not answering, the potential customer — within four minutes — opens Booking, finds your competitor 200 metres away and books there. Every reply that takes longer than fifteen minutes costs you an average of €78 in lost booking. And 64% of travellers under 45 now expect an answer in under five minutes, at any hour.

If you run a hotel or a B&B and still wake at two in the morning to answer a WhatsApp message, this guide shows how a modern AI chatbot can work in your place, sell rooms while you sleep, and save you at least twenty hours of customer care a week.

What a modern AI chatbot actually does

Forget the chatbots of 2018, with their buttons — "1 for prices, 2 for location, 3 to speak to an operator" — that frustrated people and were abandoned at the second click. An AI chatbot for hotels today is something else entirely.

A modern AI chatbot is a conversational assistant built on large language models — the same kind of technology behind ChatGPT, but trained on your property's information. It understands natural language, answers in more than 30 languages, handles complicated conversations, quotes live rates and, above all, closes the booking inside the chat, so the guest never has to leave the app they are writing in.

📌 In two lines: an AI chatbot for hotels is your digital front desk, talking to guests on WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger and your website around the clock, and turning enquiries into direct bookings with no OTA commission.

The five moments when it makes you money

This is not theory. Here are the five situations where an AI chatbot is the difference between a lost booking and money in the bank.

1. The night, when you sleep and the world books

Between 10pm and 7am roughly 37% of enquiries arrive, mostly from markets in other time zones. Without a chatbot they sit unanswered for eight or ten hours, and the customer goes elsewhere in the meantime. With one, 82% of those conversations resolve on their own, and 19% become a confirmed booking before you open your eyes.

2. Enquiries in languages you do not speak

Your team answers in Italian and English. But if a message arrives in German at 11pm, what do you do? Run it through Google Translate and hope? An AI chatbot speaks more than 30 languages fluently, colloquialisms included. The result: 22–28% more business from non-English-speaking markets.

3. The direct booking, with no OTA commission

A guest writes on WhatsApp: "Do you have a double for the weekend of the 12th?" The chatbot queries your booking engine, offers three options with rates, and closes the booking with a payment link. You save the 15–18% commission you would have paid Booking.com for the same room.

4. Upselling, automatically

While the guest is booking, the chatbot offers: breakfast in the room? An airport transfer? A guided tour of Pompeii? A good one converts 11–16% of those offers, adding an average of €32 per booking.

5. Reviews after the stay

After check-out the chatbot sends a personal message, gathers feedback privately — catching complaints before they reach TripAdvisor — and invites satisfied guests to leave a public review. On average, 45% more positive reviews collected.

AI chatbot, static FAQs or a human receptionist?

Let us compare the three options you have today for handling guest enquiries:

FeatureStatic FAQsHuman receptionistAI chatbot
Availability24/78–12 hours a day24/7
Languages1–21–330+
Understands complex questionsNoYesYes
Completes bookingsNoYes, given timeYes, automatically
Monthly cost€0€2,500–3,500€90–350
Scales to 1,000 conversations a dayBarelyImpossibleWithout trouble
Active upsellingNoInconsistentEvery time
Average response timeInstant15–90 minutes3–8 seconds
💡 A strategic note: the chatbot does not replace your receptionist. It frees them from the 200 repetitive questions a day ("Do you have a pool?", "What time is check-in?") so they can focus on what creates real value: a personal welcome, special requests, and the kind of upselling that needs a human.

How it works, technically

Here is the flow without the jargon. This is what happens when a guest writes "Do you have a room for two adults and a child from the 12th to the 15th of July?":

   ┌────────────────────┐
   │       GUEST        │
   │  writes on WhatsApp│
   └─────────┬──────────┘
             │
             ▼

   │   Large Language     │      check-in 12 Jul, check-out 15 Jul
   │       Model          │

All of this takes under eight seconds. The guest does not notice they are talking to an AI: the conversation flows, it holds context, and when it needs to, it hands over to a person without any visible seam.

The three technical pieces a real AI chatbot needs

Not everything sold as "AI" is. Here are the three building blocks that separate a toy from a working tool:

ComponentWhat it doesWhy it matters
Advanced NLP (an LLM)Understands natural language, context and typosWithout one, the chatbot misreads 40% of questions
A knowledge base of your ownHolds everything about your property: facilities, policies, photosGeneric answers send guests elsewhere
PMS and booking engine integrationConnects to your system and shows real availabilityWithout it the bot can inform, but not sell

What it costs and what it returns

The cost of a professional hospitality AI chatbot depends on features and conversation volume. Typical ranges in 2026:

  • B&Bs with 1–10 rooms: €60–120 a month (3,000–5,000 conversations)
  • Hotels with 10–30 rooms: €120–220 a month
  • Hotels with 30–80 rooms: €220–400 a month
  • 80+ rooms or chains: €400–900 a month

To tell the difference, try this: write a long, rambling question such as "I read on your site that you do breakfast but my husband is coeliac and I don't know if you have gluten-free things because he had trouble in Naples last time". If the bot answers the substance, it is AI. If it offers you buttons marked "Breakfast / Allergies / Reviews", it is a rules-based bot in disguise.

item.title: AI Dynamic Pricing: How Hotels Raise RevPAR by 35%

item.content:encoded:
The hotel 50 metres from yours sells its rooms for 28% more a night. And it fills them just the same. It does not have better rooms, a better view or better staff. It has understood one thing you have not: there is no such thing as the "right" rate. There is the right rate for that specific night, for that customer segment, at that precise moment. And an AI works it out in 0.3 seconds — not a spreadsheet updated on Sunday evening.

Seventy-one per cent of Italian hotels under 100 rooms still use static pricing, or update it by hand once a week. The result: in high-demand weeks they sell below value, and in quiet weeks they sit empty because they do not come down in time. This guide shows how an AI pricing tool realigns rates in real time and lifts RevPAR by 25–40% without cheapening the brand.

What dynamic pricing is, without the jargon

Think of airline tickets. The same Naples–Milan flight costs €49 three months out and €289 the day before. Same aircraft, same route, same service. What changes is demand at the moment you buy.

Dynamic pricing applied to hotels is exactly that: your room rate changes in real time according to dozens of variables — current demand, local events, day of the week, lead time, what competitors are doing, the weather, the customer segment. There is no "high" or "low" price: there is the price that maximises revenue at that moment.

📌 In two lines: AI dynamic pricing is software that changes your room rates automatically, every hour, to maximise RevPAR — revenue per available room. It is not about lowering prices: it is about selling at the right value at the right time.

Static, manual and AI pricing compared

Let us compare the three common approaches. The difference shows in the numbers:

FeatureStatic pricingManual pricingAI pricing
How often rates changeOnce or twice a yearOnce or twice a week24–48 times a day
Variables considered2–3 (seasonality)5–840–120
Reaction to the unexpectedNoneTwo to four days lateReal time, 15–60 minutes
Competitor analysisNoManual, occasionalAutomatic, hourly
Effect on RevPARBaseline+8–15%+25–40%
Hours of work a week0.5h6–10h1–2h of monitoring
Monthly software cost€0€0€180–700

The point is not that you spend €200 a month. The point is that with manual pricing you are leaving 20–30% of possible RevPAR on the table. On a 30-room hotel, that is €60,000–140,000 a year of revenue you never see.

Six things an AI pricing tool weighs, and you do not

When you update rates by hand you consider two or three things: the season, the weekend, maybe an event. An AI tool weighs 40 to 120 variables at once. Here are the six that matter most.

1. Current demand in the market

The AI reads live search flows on the metasearch engines — Google Hotels, Trivago, Kayak — and sees whether demand for your destination is rising. If searches for "hotel Naples 12 September" have grown 40% in the past six hours, it raises rates before you notice.

2. Local events, including ones you do not know about

Concerts, conferences, trade fairs, ceremonies. The AI has databases covering thousands of local events. If there is a medical conference in Pompeii on 23 October, it knows six months before you do and adjusts pricing for those dates.

3. What competitors are charging

The AI checks the rates of the five to fifteen competing properties you have named, every hour. If your main competitor raises prices you know within 30 minutes and respond — or deliberately stay below them to win volume.

4. The weather forecast

Weather forecasts move tourism demand by 12–18%. If sunshine is forecast over Sorrento for the weekend of 19 May while Rome has rain, searches for the coast multiply. The AI knows ten days ahead.

5. Lead time

The rate curve has to respond to how many days remain. A room still free three days before check-in is worth less — or more, depending on the occupancy curve — than one sold 60 days out. The AI manages that curve with surgical precision.

6. Customer segment

The AI recognises whether the request comes from a leisure guest (weekend, family) or a business one (midweek, single). It adjusts the price and offers different restrictions: minimum stay, packages.

How it works, technically

Here is the simplified flow of one rate-update cycle:

   │   DATA SOURCES (INPUT)   │
   ├──────────────────────────┤
   │ • PMS (occupancy)        │

   │   OUTPUT: NEW RATES      │
   │   per room type          │
   │   per date               │
   └──────────────┬───────────┘

   ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │   CHANNEL MANAGER        │ ◄── publishes to

All of this happens 24 to 48 times a day, automatically. You only see the bookings arrive and the revenue grow month on month.

The AI pricing tools worth considering in 2026

The market offers different answers depending on the size and kind of property. These are the ones we see working best in Italy, with indicative prices:

Where the +35% RevPAR actually comes from

Plenty of hoteliers stay sceptical. "+35% RevPAR sounds like marketing." Let us see where it comes from, with real numbers. A 50-room hotel, average ADR €130, occupancy 65%:

In other words: for every €1 spent on AI pricing you recover 95 in extra revenue. The return shows by the second month.

A real case: a 50-room hotel on the Amalfi Coast

A four-star hotel in Praiano, 50 rooms, open from April to November, family-run. Starting point (2024 season):

  • Rates updated by hand by the manager, twice a week
  • Three standard rates: low, mid and high season
  • Competitor pricing checked by eye once a week
  • No analysis of local events or weather
  • Average ADR €165, occupancy 71%, RevPAR €117

  2. Software choice: Atomize, for the level of sophistication required
  3. PMS and channel manager integration: two-way data connection
  4. Brand limits defined: a psychological floor price — never below €140 — and packaging rules
  5. Competitor set: eleven competing properties identified for continuous benchmarking
  6. Events calendar: 380 relevant local events loaded (the Ravello Festival, Easter, long weekends and the rest)
  7. Team training: twelve hours on the dashboard and on manual overrides

The AI sees patterns I cannot, because I am looking at 50 rooms and it is looking at 50,000 hotels like mine. The 2025 season changed my career." — Revenue manager, Amalfi Coast hotel (50 rooms)

Implementing it in 45 days: the checklist

Weeks 1–2 — Audit and choice of software

  1. Export 24 months of booking history from the PMS
  2. Analyse ADR, occupancy and RevPAR by month and by room type
  3. Identify the competitor set: eight to fifteen properties
  4. Map the relevant local events calendar, at least 24 months of it
  5. Take free demos of three shortlisted tools
  6. Choose on budget and features

Week 3 — Technical integration

  1. Two-way connection with the PMS
  2. Connection with the channel manager, to publish rates
  3. Connection with the booking engine on your own site
  4. Test synchronisation on a single room
  5. Check the reporting and KPI dashboard

Week 4 — Strategy configuration

  1. Set minimum and maximum prices — your brand guardrails
  2. Configure packaging rules (BAR, advance purchase, non-refundable)
  3. Set up the competitor set for monitoring
  4. Load the local events calendar
  5. Define your priority customer segments

Weeks 5–6 — Launch and tuning

  1. Launch in shadow mode: the AI suggests, the revenue manager approves
  2. After two weeks, switch to fully automatic
  3. Daily KPI monitoring for the first four weeks
  4. Tune the algorithm against real results
  5. Weekly revenue-against-budget reporting
⚠️ Mind your brand's price floor: never let the AI drop below the minimum your positioning can bear. A four-star Amalfi Coast hotel selling at €89 in November to fill rooms destroys its perceived value for the following season. Always set hard guardrails and let the AI optimise inside that range. Dynamic pricing is not discounting: it is maximising revenue at rates consistent with your brand.

The three most common mistakes

  1. Not integrating it with the channel manager. The AI works out the optimal rate, but if it is not published automatically on every channel you lose 70% of the value. Without integration you are back to manual pricing.
  2. Not loading local events. The AI has international databases, but Italian local events — village festivals, patron saints' days, regional festivals — have to be taught to it. Without a local calendar it misses the most profitable dates.
  3. Emotional overrides. After two good weeks the revenue manager "has a feeling" and reverses the rates by hand. The AI works if you let it work. Override on data, never on instinct.

Related reading

  • Channel managers for hotels: the complete 2026 guide — a channel manager is the technical prerequisite for any dynamic pricing strategy
  • AI chatbots for hotels and B&Bs: the 24/7 digital front desk — chatbot plus pricing AI is the full stack
  • How to avoid overbooking: a practical guide — overbooking wipes out the gains from dynamic pricing

In closing: manual pricing is your largest hidden cost

When a hotelier tells me "dynamic pricing costs €300 a month and I am not sure I can afford it", my answer is always the same: you cannot afford to be without it. Because every month of delay is a month spent selling below value when demand is high and sitting empty when it is low. It is the classic invisible cost: you never see it on an invoice, you pay it every day.

In 2026 AI dynamic pricing is no longer frontier technology: it is an industry standard, exactly as the booking engine was a novelty in 2010 and is now a requirement. Falling behind here is measured in years, not months, because whoever starts now compounds revenue that manual pricing will never recover.

item.title: Sustainable Tourism 2026: Green Certifications, KPIs and Eco-Conscious Travellers
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Seventy-three per cent of travellers (Booking, 2025) say sustainability is a deciding factor when choosing a hotel. Yet only 12% of Italian properties hold a recognised environmental certification. In plain terms: you are losing bookings to a competitor with a green badge on your own street. And while you think "I will do it later", they raise their average rate by 18% and take 27% more revenue from the international family segment.

If you run a hotel, a B&B or a resort in Campania, this guide explains how to turn sustainability from a perceived cost into a commercial lever: which certifications actually count, what they cost, which measures pay back fastest, and how to talk about them without falling into greenwashing.

What "sustainable tourism" really means

Let us be clear from the start: sustainable tourism is not a sign with a green leaf at reception. It is a way of operating that reduces the property's impact on the environment, the local community and the regional economy — and proves it with measurable KPIs and certifications verified by an external body.

The UN World Tourism Organization defines it as "tourism that takes full account of its current and future economic, social and environmental impacts, addressing the needs of visitors, the industry, the environment and host communities".

📌 In two lines: sustainability in tourism means measuring consumption — water, energy, waste — reducing it through concrete measures, certifying the results with an outside body and reporting them transparently. Everything else is empty marketing, and today reviewers expose it within 48 hours.

The three dimensions

A serious approach rests on three pillars. Skip one and you are exposed to greenwashing accusations from better-informed travellers.

1. Environmental

The most visible: energy, water, waste, CO₂ emissions, biodiversity. It covers LED lighting, solar panels, flow restrictors, going plastic-free, proper recycling and food-waste tracking.

2. Social

This concerns workers' rights — proper contracts, training, gender equality — the relationship with the community (local suppliers, regional events, accessibility) and the host culture (traditions, language, craftsmanship).

3. Economic

Sustainability has to be financially sound: measures need a demonstrable return, the property has to stay competitive, and the revenue should circulate locally through nearby suppliers and local employment.

The main international certifications compared

There are over 200 "green" certifications in tourism. Most are useless: little visibility, opaque criteria, no OTA recognition. These five are the ones that matter for the Italian and international market.

CertificationAverage costValidityMain criteriaOTA recognition
Green Key€600–1,800/year1 year, renewable13 areas: environmental management, guest involvement, water, energy, waste, foodBooking, Expedia (dedicated badge)
Travelife€350–1,200/year2 years200+ GSTC criteria, on-site audit, supply chainBooking ("Travel Sustainable Level 3" badge)
EU Ecolabel€800–2,000 plus an annual fee3–5 yearsEU standard: 22 mandatory criteria plus 67 optionalBooking, Expedia, dedicated EU site
EarthCheck€2,500–8,000/year1 year, with annual auditBenchmarking across 10 KPIs, scientific certificationPremium market, hotel chains
Blue Flag (coastal resorts)€350–900/year1 yearWater quality, environmental management, services, educationInstitutional recognition (FEE)
💡 A strategic note: for a B&B or a hotel under 30 rooms, start with Green Key. It is the most affordable, it has the broadest OTA recognition, and the process is manageable in four to six months. EU Ecolabel comes later, once your processes are settled.

The ten measures with the best return

You do not do sustainability all at once. You start with what pays back fastest and reinvest the savings in the next step. Here is the sequence we use with clients.

MeasureAverage cost (30-room hotel)PaybackImpact
1. LED lighting throughout€3,500–6,00014–18 months−65% lighting electricity
2. Smart thermostats per room€4,000–8,00016–24 months−22% climate control
3. Plastic-free (refillable amenities, no small bottles)€1,500–3,000 setup8–12 months−90% single-use plastic
4. Local suppliers for food and drink+8–15% initial food costOffset by premium pricing−40% food transport emissions
5. Towel and linen policy€0–500 (cards)Immediate−30% laundry
6. Solar panels (20–30 kWp)€25,000–40,0005–7 years−60% electricity bill
7. Food waste tracking (Winnow and similar)€2,000/year12 months−35% kitchen waste
8. EV charging points for guests€3,500–7,00024–36 months, plus extra leadsDifferentiation and premium segment
9. Water flow restrictors€800–1,5006–9 months−35% water use
10. Certified green electricity+5–12% on the billOffset by pricing and the badge−100% Scope 2 emissions

Adding up the first six on a 30-room hotel means a total investment of roughly €40,000–65,000, with an aggregate payback of 28 to 36 months — before counting the extra occupancy and higher average rate that eco positioning brings.

Experiences Srl surveys your property, identifies what pays back fastest, takes you through to Green Key, Travelife or EU Ecolabel certification, and sets up how it is communicated on your site, the OTAs and social. Sustainability that generates bookings, not just a brochure.

Public funding available in 2026

The objection we hear most often is "it costs too much". The technical answer is that the net cost, after incentives and tax relief, averages 35–45% of the gross. Here are the schemes that matter most to a property in Campania.

  • Transizione 5.0 tax credit: 35–45% on coordinated investments in energy efficiency and digitisation, until 31 December 2026
  • Conto Termico 3.0: direct incentives for heat pumps, solar thermal and energy retrofits, paid annually over up to five years
  • POR FESR Campania, sustainable tourism strand: grants of up to 50% on combined efficiency and certification projects
  • Ecobonus 65% on energy efficiency work: heat pumps, windows, solar shading
  • Appliance bonus: 50% on class A or higher appliances
  • National recovery plan, tourism strand: a dedicated call for sustainability certification, with funds remaining in 2026

On a gross investment of €50,000 in eco measures, an average property recovers €18,000–22,000 across tax credits, bonuses and regional grants. The real net cost falls to €28,000–32,000, with payback in 24 to 30 months.

How Booking, Airbnb and Expedia reward certified properties

The OTAs are not environmental charities: they do this because their algorithms show that users convert better on certified properties. Here is how it works, platform by platform.

Booking.com — Travel Sustainable programme

Since 2022 Booking has awarded a "Travel Sustainable" badge at three levels, according to how many criteria you meet — from five basic ones to more than twenty advanced. An external certification such as Green Key or Travelife takes you straight to Level 3, the highest. Level 3 properties get:

  • Priority placement in the eco filters, used by 41% of European users in 2025
  • A badge visible in search results and on the property page
  • A dedicated slot in themed marketing emails
  • 18% higher click-through on average than uncertified properties

Airbnb — sustainability filters

Airbnb has introduced "renewable energy", "eco transport" and "minimal waste" filters in search. Properties that declare — with documentary evidence — that they meet them appear earlier in results and in personalised feeds. The Plus segment gives further priority to externally certified hosts.

Expedia Group — sustainable hotel filter

Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo share a "Sustainable" filter. To be included you need a GSTC-recognised certification — Green Key, Travelife, EU Ecolabel and EarthCheck all qualify. The filter is used by 28% of American travellers coming to Europe.

A real case: an 8-room B&B in Positano, Green Key in six months

A family B&B in Positano, eight rooms, run by a young couple, with mostly American and northern European guests. Starting point (January 2025):

  1. Initial audit: mapped consumption, suppliers, processes and the gaps against the Green Key criteria
  2. Quick wins: LED throughout, water flow restrictors, refillable dispensers instead of single-use amenities, a towel and linen policy with bilingual cards
  3. Local suppliers: renegotiated contracts with three producers within 20 km — coffee, preserves, tomatoes
  4. Certified green electricity: switched to a supplier with 100% guarantees of origin
  5. A small solar array: 6 kWp on the roof, with a 40% regional grant
  6. KPI measurement: dedicated water and energy meters plus food-waste tracking
  7. Green Key documentation: self-assessment completed, on-site audit, certificate obtained in June 2025
  8. Communication: a new "sustainability story" page, updated OTA profiles, a badge on the site, the story told on Instagram

Results after 12 months (January 2025 → January 2026)
