"We thought we were investing in 'the right thing to do'. Four months in we realised it was also a brilliant commercial decision: Americans arrive already knowing we are Green Key, they stay longer, they spend more with our local tour partners, and they leave three-paragraph reviews. The solar panels paid for themselves in two seasons thanks to higher rates, not only the lower bill." — Anna and Marco, owners of an 8-room B&B in Positano

How to talk about it without sounding hollow

The measures alone are not enough: badly communicated, they become cost without extra revenue. Three practical rules we apply with clients.

1. Tell the story in numbers, not adjectives

Wrong: "We are an environmentally conscious property." Right: "We cut our energy consumption by 58% in 2025 with a 6 kWp solar array and 100% LED lighting. That is the equivalent of taking four cars off the road for a year."

2. A dedicated sustainability page

A page on your site with: the certifications you hold, with official badges; your annual KPIs, published; a list of local suppliers by name, with a map; real photographs of the work, not stock images; and the person responsible, with a name, not "our team".

3. Weave it into the stay

A bilingual card in the room with the three things a guest can do to help ("reuse your towel: you save 60 litres of water and 0.4 kWh"), a QR code to the sustainability page, and pre-stay and post-stay emails showing their personal impact.

A 90-day roadmap to start well

Weeks 1–2 — Audit and benchmark

  1. Collect 24 months of bills: electricity, gas, water, waste
  2. Map current suppliers and distances
  3. Inventory amenities and single-use products
  4. Calculate baseline consumption per occupied room

Weeks 3–4 — Quick wins

  1. Replace all lighting with LED
  2. Install flow restrictors
  3. Towel and linen policy with bilingual cards
  4. Remove single-use plastic: bottles, amenities

Weeks 5–8 — Structural work

  1. Smart thermostats per room, with presence sensors
  2. Switch to certified green electricity
  3. Select three to five priority local suppliers
  4. Set up food waste tracking

Weeks 9–12 — Certification and communication

  1. Begin the Green Key process with the self-assessment
  2. Photographic documentation and written procedures
  3. Build the sustainability page on your site
  4. Update OTA profiles with certifiable data
  5. Train the team on how to talk to guests about it
  6. The Green Key on-site audit
   ┌──────────────────┐
   │   MONTH 1        │  Audit + quick wins
   │ LED, water,      │  Investment: ~€5,000
   │ policy, plastic  │  Savings: already measurable
   └────────┬─────────┘
            ▼
   ┌──────────────────┐
   │   MONTH 2        │  Structural work
   │ Smart thermostats│  Investment: ~€10,000
   │ Green electricity│  Savings: −30% energy
   │ Local suppliers  │  The story begins
   └────────┬─────────┘
            ▼
   ┌──────────────────┐
   │   MONTH 3        │  Certification + launch
   │ Green Key process│  External audit
   │ Communication    │  OTA badge live
   │ Team training    │  Measurable results
   └──────────────────┘
⚠️ Greenwashing does more harm than good. Real cases: an Italian resort claimed "100% plastic-free" in 2024 while serving drinks in PET bottles — a guest posted the video, it reached the TripAdvisor front page, and reviews fell from 4.6 to 3.9 in two months. A Tuscan hotel declared itself "carbon neutral" without evidence; a journalist exposed it, fourteen negative articles followed and the offsetting partner withdrew. The golden rule: if you do not have an external certification and measurable KPIs, do not claim it. Talk about the individual measures — LED, local sourcing, green electricity — but never make a total claim.

  • Local SEO for hotels: reaching Google's top three in 90 days — why ranking for "sustainable hotel [city]" is a commercially valuable keyword
  • Smart hotels: keyless check-in, smart keys and IoT — the technical pillar that pairs with sustainability
  • Channel managers for tour operators — how to monetise the eco-conscious segment on local experiences too

In closing: sustainability is now the strongest differentiator

Two things will happen over the next 36 months. Eco-conscious travellers will move from 73% "interested" to more than half who "will not book without proof", and the OTAs will make sustainability filters prevail in default results. Whoever starts today reaches that line with the accounts already in order, the certifications in hand and higher average rates. Whoever waits will be chasing — at higher cost and with less credibility.

The good news: the payback is proven, the incentives are still generous, and the combination of measures, certification and communication generates extra revenue well beyond the cost. In 2026 sustainability is no longer an ethical choice: it is a business decision.

item.title: Smart Hotels: Keyless Check-In, Smart Keys and In-Room IoT
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A traditional check-in costs your hotel €18–22 per guest once you add up staff time, desk occupancy, typing errors, queues and dead time. Across 10,000 arrivals a year that is €200,000 burnt on a process 64% of guests say they would "avoid if they could" (Skift Research, 2025). And while you print paper forms, the competitor 500 metres away already has check-in running from a phone, an NPS of 78 and no queue at six in the evening.

If you run a hotel of 30 rooms or more, this guide sets out what "smart hotel" actually means in 2026: which technologies are genuinely needed, what they cost, what they return, and how to implement keyless check-in, smart keys and in-room IoT in 90 days — without sacrificing the human welcome.

What a smart hotel really is

Let us clear away the cliché: a smart hotel is not a hotel full of robots. It is a property where the low-value processes are automated and the high-value ones — the relationship with the guest, solving problems, the experience — are strengthened by technology. There are four operational dimensions.

1. Check-in and check-out

Online pre-check-in, document upload, digital signature, payment, smart key delivery. Average time spent at the property: from 11 minutes to 90 seconds.

2. The in-room experience

Smart thermostat, adaptive lighting, voice assistant, a smart TV the guest can log into with their own Netflix account, a control tablet, personalised scenes: relax, work, sleep.

3. Energy and operations

Presence sensors that switch off climate control and lights, window sensors that stop the air conditioning, a central energy dashboard, predictive maintenance.

4. Data and personalisation

A unified CRM, segmentation, automatic messaging before, during and after the stay, intelligent upselling, dynamic pricing based on real demand.

📌 In two lines: a smart hotel is not technology in every corner. It is invisible technology that removes friction for the guest and cost for the property. If the guest notices it, it is probably badly designed.

How keyless check-in actually works

The ideal flow of a fully digital check-in looks like this:

  ┌─────────────────┐
  │     BOOKING     │  From an OTA or your own site
  │   Booking/Site  │
  └────────┬────────┘
           │
           ▼ (48h before arrival)
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  CHECK-IN LINK  │  Automatic email and SMS
  │  by email/SMS   │
  └────────┬────────┘
           │
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  ID UPLOAD +    │  Photo of the document + selfie
  │  VERIFICATION   │  AI checks the match
  └────────┬────────┘
           │
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  PAYMENT +      │  Tokenised card
  │  E-SIGNATURE    │  Privacy form
  └────────┬────────┘
           │
           ▼ (day of arrival)
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │   SMART KEY     │  Code + app + NFC
  │    delivered    │  Sent two hours ahead
  └────────┬────────┘
           │
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  GUEST ENTERS   │  No contact with reception
  │   THEIR ROOM    │  Time taken: 90 seconds
  └─────────────────┘

None of this requires the front desk to type anything: identity data is transmitted automatically to the authorities through the national guest reporting system, the invoice is generated and the PMS is updated.

The five main platforms in the Italian market

Not every solution is equivalent. These are the five most dependable for Italy in 2026.

Smart keys: NFC, PIN code or app?

Three technologies dominate. Choosing well affects security, the guest experience and replacement costs.

NFC cardA traditional RFID card, rewritten at each check-in from the PMSFamiliar, robust, no app neededCard cost, cloning (rare)Good, thanks to key rotation

App / BluetoothA dedicated app opens the door over Bluetooth or phone NFCA premium experience, and can control lights and climate tooRequires installing an app, depends on the phoneHigh: encryption, biometric unlock
💡 A strategic note: do not pick one technology. Always offer two — for example a PIN code by default plus an app for those who want it. A share of guests, especially over 60, will never install an app for a two-night stay. Forcing them costs you reviews.

In-room IoT: what is worth it and what is not

IoT marketing will sell you anything. In practice, these are the devices with a real effect on return and experience.

Take a 40-room hotel, 70% occupancy, 10,200 arrivals a year, average rate €130. Here are the real numbers.

A real case: a 60-room four-star on Ischia, implemented in 90 days

A four-star hotel on Ischia, 60 rooms, mostly European families and couples, open March to November. Starting point (January 2025):

  • Reception staffed around the clock across three shifts, 3.5 FTE
  • Average check-in time: 11 minutes, peaking at 40 in high season
  • NPS: 54
  • Room energy costs: €68,000 a year
  • Booking reviews: 8.4, with "slow check-in" the main complaint

What we did in 90 days

  1. Audit: analysed the check-in process, reception flows and network infrastructure
  2. Platform chosen: Selfit, for its native integration with the existing Hotelcube system
  3. Smart locks: fitted on all 60 rooms, with NFC, code and app
  4. Smart thermostats: 60 units with presence sensors
  5. Window sensors: stopping the air conditioning when a window opens
  6. Guest reporting integration: automatic transmission of documents to the authorities
  7. Samsung Hospitality smart TVs: in every room, with guest Netflix login
  8. Team training: 1.5 FTE moved from reception to "guest experience manager"
  9. Pre-arrival messaging: a new email and SMS flow with the check-in link 48 hours ahead

Results after 12 months (January 2025 → January 2026)

Total season revenue€2,180,000€2,620,000+€440,000
"My biggest fear was 'what if a guest wants to talk to someone?'. It turned out to be unfounded: whoever wants us finds us in the lobby. The rest — the majority — are happy not to queue after six hours on a plane. We moved a receptionist to 'experience host' and today she is the most in-demand person in the hotel: tour bookings, restaurant advice, solving problems on the spot. Check-in was never hospitality. It was paperwork." — Manager, four-star hotel on Ischia (60 rooms)

The most common mistakes

Across four years of smart hotel projects, these five repeat with worrying regularity. Knowing them in advance saves months.

1. Buying hardware before choosing the software

The classic: the owner orders 60 smart locks because they were on offer, then discovers they do not integrate with the chosen platform. The result: hardware to resell and four months lost. The rule: choose the platform first, then the hardware the vendor certifies.

2. Underestimating the network

Smart locks, thermostats, sensors and TVs need stable Wi-Fi, segmented so guest traffic and IoT traffic are on separate networks, with coverage in every corner. An investment of €3,000–8,000 in professional access points is almost always necessary in older Italian buildings.

3. No fallback for the guest who cannot or will not

There will always be guests who cannot or do not want to use digital check-in. You need a clear alternative: a person available, a valid printed code in an envelope, an emergency number. Without one, a frustrated guest leaves a one-star review.

4. Cutting staff instead of redeploying them

A smart hotel does not reduce people, it reduces low-value tasks. Properties that made their reception redundant saw NPS fall by 12 to 18 points. Properties that redeployed those roles as guest experience hosts saw it rise by 20 to 25.

5. Not measuring before launch

Without a baseline — current check-in time, current NPS, current energy costs — you cannot show the return. Measure for at least 30 days before starting. That data is what will convince you to carry on through the inevitable hiccups of the first month.

Privacy and GDPR

A smart hotel collects sensitive data: documents, optionally biometrics, behaviour. Compliance is not optional.

  • Facial recognition: only on a strong legal basis with explicit consent; it must be optional and never the only way in
  • Biometric data: a special category under article 9 GDPR, requiring a data protection impact assessment
  • Document retention: a maximum of 30 days for the copy; beyond that, only the metadata required by the authorities
  • Encryption: required both in transit and at rest for identity data
  • A multilingual privacy notice: clear, available before check-in, with non-digital alternatives offered
  • Vendor due diligence: make sure the platform is GDPR-compliant with servers in the EU
⚠️ Smart does not mean cold. The biggest risk of a smart hotel is feeling dehumanised. The golden rule: automate what the guest does not want to do, not what they enjoy doing. Check-in is in the first group — nobody loves a queue. A restaurant recommendation is in the second. Keep a human host for the welcome, problem solving and relationships, ideally redeployed from reception rather than removed. Properties that eliminated every human presence saw NPS and reviews collapse within twelve months.

Implementation roadmap: six months to a complete system

Month 1 — Audit and platform choice

  1. Map the existing check-in and check-out processes
  2. Audit the network: Wi-Fi in rooms, coverage
  3. Shortlist three platforms and take demos
  4. Check integration with your existing PMS
  5. Choose the vendor and sign

Month 2 — Software setup

  1. Configure the check-in platform
  2. Integrate the PMS and the guest reporting system
  3. Set up the pre-arrival email and SMS flow
  4. Test with internal bookings

Months 3–4 — In-room hardware

  1. Install smart locks, testing on five pilot rooms first
  2. Smart thermostats and presence sensors
  3. Window sensors
  4. Smart TVs, if planned
  5. Roll out across every room

Month 5 — Training and the new operating model

  1. Train the team on the new flow
  2. Redeploy reception roles into guest experience
  3. Backup procedures: what to do when a guest cannot manage the technology
  4. Soft launch on direct bookings

Month 6 — Launch and tuning

  1. Launch across every channel
  2. Weekly KPI monitoring
  3. Tune on guest feedback
  4. Communicate it on the OTAs and your site with a "smart check-in" badge

What it really costs: three realistic scenarios

For a rough reference, here are three realistic configurations with everything included — software, hardware, setup and training, before any incentives.

ScenarioConfigurationYear one investmentAnnual fee
Starter (B&B or hotel, 10–20 rooms)Digital check-in, smart locks, automatic guest reporting, email flow€12,000–22,000€3,600–5,400
Standard (hotel, 30–60 rooms)The above plus smart thermostats, window sensors, smart TVs and a CRM€48,000–78,000€7,200–12,000
Premium (4–5 star, over 60 rooms)The above plus voice assistants, room scenes, an energy dashboard and a digital concierge€110,000–180,000€18,000–28,000

With the Transizione 5.0 tax credit, available until 31 December 2026, and regional tourism grants, the real net cost of the initial investment falls on average by 35–50%. On a €60,000 Standard setup that means €30,000–36,000 in practice. Average payback stays within 22 to 28 months.

Related reading

If this was useful, read also:

  • Channel managers for hotels: the complete 2026 guide — the first technical building block, from which every smart hotel project starts
  • AI chatbots for hotels and B&Bs — how to complete the experience with a concierge that answers around the clock in 30 languages
  • Sustainable tourism and green certifications — smart plus green is the most profitable positioning in the international market

In closing: the smart hotel is not the future, it is the present

In 2026 keyless check-in is already in place at 41% of international chains in Italy and 22% of independent hotels over 50 rooms. In plain terms: if you do not start now, you will start from behind. The advantage held by those who invested early shows up as higher NPS, lower operating costs, better ADR and — above all — reviews that talk about a modern experience rather than a queue at reception.

The technology is mature, the Italian vendors are solid, and the incentives bring the hardware cost down. The right moment to implement was twelve months ago. The second best is now.

item.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality for Tour Operators: Selling the Experience Before It Happens
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A traveller who previews the tour they are considering is 67% more likely to book (Skift, 2025). Are you still showing them a gallery of static photographs taken four years ago, perhaps with the photographer's watermark and a grey November sky? Then every month you are handing over dozens of customers who see the same experience presented immersively on a competitor's site and book there without ever hearing of you.

Virtual reality and augmented reality are no longer trade-show gadgets: they have become measurable sales tools, within reach of a tour operator with ten or twenty staff, with a demonstrable effect on conversion and average order value. This guide covers what you need to know in 2026 to stop describing the experience and start letting people try it before they pay.

VR and AR: the difference in two lines

Before the numbers, let us settle the terms. This is not jargon: it is what you need to talk to a supplier without being sold smoke, and to point the budget at the right thing.

Virtual reality (VR)

VR replaces what the traveller sees. They put on a headset, or look through a phone in 360° mode, and find themselves inside your tour: the excavations at Pompeii, the summit of Vesuvius, the alleys of Procida. It is isolated, total, immersive. It works beautifully as a pre-sale tool because it answers the international traveller's main objection: "will it really be as they say?"

Augmented reality (AR)

AR adds digital elements to the real world. The traveller points their phone at a Roman forum and sees it on screen as it was 2,000 years ago, with statues, intact columns and animated merchants. You are not replacing reality, you are enriching it. For a tour operator it is the simplest way to justify a premium ticket: the perceived experience scales while the marginal cost stays flat.

Mixed reality, for completeness

You increasingly hear about MR (Apple Vision Pro, Meta Quest 3) — a hybrid where virtual objects interact with the real environment. For now it is a niche market, a few hundred thousand headsets in Italy, so give it no more than a coffee's worth of attention until device prices fall below €500.

📌 In two lines: VR works before the booking, letting people try the tour from home. AR works during the tour, raising perceived value and justifying a higher price. Two different levers, at two different points in the funnel.

The four use cases that actually work

Ignore the noise about the "tourism metaverse". These are the four applications generating measurable bookings today.

1. Previewing the tour from home (360° VR)

From the sofa, the traveller puts on a Meta Quest headset or simply opens the 360° video on your site from their phone. They see, first-hand, the fifteen key minutes of the tour: entering the archaeological park, the guide explaining, the panoramic view at the end. They are not reading a description: they are having a sensory preview.

Measured effect on Italian tour operators that added VR previews in 2024–2025:

  • Average time on the product page: from 1:20 to 4:35
  • Conversion rate: +38–42%
  • Cart abandonment: −22%
  • Refunds after the tour: −19%, because the traveller already knows what to expect and avoids a bad impulse purchase

2. AR during the tour (historical overlay)

Walking among the ruins, the traveller opens an app or scans a QR code. The screen shows a 3D reconstruction of what they are looking at, with the guide's audio, explanatory pop-ups and animated historical figures. Missing statues reappear. Walls return to their original painted splendour. The noise of the forum, the footsteps of senators, the market traders.

The commercial consequence: you can sell the same tour as a premium experience at 30–50% above the base ticket. Pure margin, because the marginal cost per traveller is only software. And it produces a second, quieter advantage: a traveller who has had an AR experience is 2.4 times more likely to leave a positive review with photographs (TripAdvisor, 2025), which in turn drives new conversions at no cost.

3. Walking around locations (immersive street view)

Virtual tours in the manner of Google Street View, but yours and built to sell. The traveller can walk through the village, turn the view, click points of interest that open as product cards. It works very well for:

  • City tours — underground Naples, the Spanish Quarter, the historic centre
  • Visits to wineries, farms and agriturismi
  • Previews of cruises and boat trips, showing the interiors

4. Previews that drive upselling

The traveller is about to book the standard Vesuvius tour at €45. You show them, in VR, the difference between the basic entry — a group of 30, a 40-minute wait — and the "skip the line plus sunset" option at €78. Seeing the difference, 31% upgrade. Without the preview, only 7% do.

The principle works because VR makes tangible a difference that stays abstract in text or a photograph. "Sunset over the crater" is words; thirty seconds of panoramic view in warm light is a feeling. The second one sells. The first is skipped.

Three ways, from simplest to most sophisticated:

1. An HTML5 iframe (five minutes)

2. Self-hosted 360° video

Upload the video to YouTube or Vimeo in 360° mode and use the native player. No cost, but you lose the advanced tracking: hotspot clicks, where people looked.

3. A native app with an AR SDK

AR during the tour needs an iOS and Android app built with ARKit or ARCore. Cost: €8,000–20,000 for the first release, plus maintenance. Only worth it if you sell 200 or more tickets a day.

  1. Choose the three or four bestsellers to convert to VR
  2. Pick the platform: Klapty to start cheaply, ThingLink for tracking

item.title: Voice Search for Hotels: Optimising for Alexa and Google Assistant
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
When a traveller asks "Alexa, find me a hotel near Vesuvius with a pool under €120", Alexa reads out one result. Not the top three. Not the first page of Google. One. If it is not yours, you have lost that booking — and more than that: you have lost even the awareness that you existed. The traveller does not know they did not choose you. To them you are simply invisible.

In 2026, 27% of travel searches are already spoken, and Gartner estimates half will be by 2027. If you run a hotel and have not optimised your site for Alexa, Google Assistant and Siri, you are losing half of a market that is forming right now. This is the complete guide to turning that around, with every technical and strategic step.

What voice search is actually worth in tourism

Let us start with real numbers, not fanciful projections.

  • 27% of travel searches in 2025 are spoken (Adobe Digital Insights)
  • 50% expected by 2027 (Gartner and PhocusWire)
  • 18% higher average order value on hotel bookings that start from voice search compared with typed search — the voice user is further along the decision, less of a window shopper
  • 74% of voice users never go past the first result — literally cannot, because Alexa or Google Assistant read them only one
  • 1.2 billion smart speakers active worldwide at the end of 2025

Put commercially: if you are not the result that gets read out for the spoken queries about your area, you have an acquisition channel potentially worth thousands of euros a month that, for you, simply does not exist.

How a voice search really works

Drop the idea that voice search is "Google, but you talk". It is a different thing. The flow is this.

1. Intent recognition

Alexa or Google work out what the user actually wants. "Find me a hotel" is commercial intent; "what time is it in Naples" is informational. On commercial intent, the engine favours transactional results: booking engines, OTAs, Google Business Profile.

2. Natural language processing

The system extracts the key entities: type of property (hotel), location (near Vesuvius), constraints (with a pool, under €120). Each becomes a filter.

3. Knowledge graph and featured snippets

Google draws on its Knowledge Graph — Business Profile, schema markup, structured data — and on featured snippets. Alexa mostly pulls from Bing and Amazon partners. Siri from Google and Apple Maps.

4. The single-answer paradigm

The system picks one answer. It reads it aloud. That is all. There is no page two. There are no other results. There is one winning answer, and everything else has lost.

📌 In two lines: optimising for voice search means designing every page of your site to be "the single right answer" to a specific spoken question. No longer ranking in the top ten: being the answer.

Seven ways voice SEO differs from the traditional kind

Understanding these is the prerequisite for any strategy. Spoken queries are a different species from typed ones.

AspectTraditional SEOVoice SEO
Query length2–4 words7–12 words
FormBare keywordsConversational sentences
IntentOften exploratoryAlmost always transactional or navigational
LocationImplicitExplicit ("near me", "here in Naples")
MomentPlanningRight here, right now
Winning positionsTop tenPosition one and the featured snippet only
DeviceDesktop or phone screenSmart speaker, hands-free phone, car

Ten examples: spoken against typed

Here is the difference in practice, applied to hotels:

Typed querySpoken query
hotel naples centre"Find me a hotel in the historic centre of Naples with breakfast included"
hotel vesuvius pool"Alexa, is there a hotel with a pool near Vesuvius under 120 euros?"
b&b posillipo sea view"Hey Google, what's a B&B with a sea view in Posillipo for two nights"
pet friendly hotel naples"I'm looking for a hotel in Naples where I can bring my dog"
4 star hotel ischia"What are the best four-star hotels on Ischia with a spa"
hotel parking naples"Find me a hotel in Naples with free parking"
wedding hotel sorrento"Wedding hotels in Sorrento with a coastal view"
family hotel procida"A hotel suitable for families with children on Procida"
last minute hotel capri"Is there a hotel available tonight on Capri under 200 euros"
boutique hotel chiaia"What's a luxury boutique hotel in Chiaia, Naples"

Notice the pattern: spoken queries are complete questions, with explicit constraints — price, duration, facilities, proximity. Your site has to contain these phrases as questions and answers, literally.

The golden rule: optimise for featured snippets

Google reads aloud from featured snippets — the boxes at the top of results — in 70% of cases. Win the snippet and you win voice search for that query.

How do you win one? By answering the question as concisely and clearly as possible, in the first part of the page:

  • A direct answer of 40–60 words immediately under an H2 that restates the question
  • Bulleted or numbered lists after the answer
  • FAQPage schema where the page is organised as questions and answers
  • Simple language, short sentences, subject-verb-object

How to structure the site

Four technical layers. All necessary, none sufficient on its own.

1. LocalBusiness, Hotel and FAQPage schema (not optional)

Without schema markup you are invisible to voice. The minimum:

  • Hotel schema: name, address, phone, star rating, facilities (pool, parking, wifi, breakfast, pet-friendly), check-in and check-out, price range
  • LocalBusiness schema: opening hours, area served, GPS coordinates
  • FAQPage schema: for every strategic question with a short answer
  • Review schema: aggregateRating with score and review count

2. An FAQ section on every service page

Every page — home, rooms, restaurant, spa, location — needs an FAQ section with questions in natural language:

  • "Is the hotel pet friendly?"
  • "How far is Naples central station?"
  • "Is breakfast included?"
  • "Can I check in after 10pm?"

3. Microdata for address, phone and hours

Your name, address and phone must be identical everywhere: site, Google Business Profile, TripAdvisor, OTAs, social. A single discrepancy in a phone number is enough to lose the engines' confidence.

4. Page speed under two seconds

Google penalises slow sites for voice, because a voice user is impatient — driving, hands busy, wanting an answer now. Target: LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms.

Five things to do this week

You do not need a large budget or a rewrite of the site. Five targeted steps, doable in seven days, already put you in contention.

1. Add an FAQ section to every product and service page

At least six to eight questions per page, in natural language — "Can I…?", "Is there…?", "How far is…?" — with answers of 40 to 60 words.

2. Implement complete schema markup

Hotel, LocalBusiness, FAQPage and Review. Validate with Google's Rich Results Test before publishing. Bad schema does more harm than none.

3. Rewrite headings so they can be answered in a sentence

Old: "Deluxe rooms". New: "Our deluxe rooms in central Naples: what they include and what they cost". The heading should contain the answer to the likely question.

4. Complete your Google Business Profile

Recent photographs — at least 40 — a 750-character description rich in spoken-query language, up-to-date hours, and a Q&A section you populate yourself. Weekly posts help further.

5. Build location-intent pages

For example: "How to reach our hotel from Naples airport", "What to do near our hotel in 24 hours", "Hotels five minutes from Naples central station". These catch geographic spoken queries with very high intent.

The complete voice intent flow

   ┌────────────────────┐
   │ TRAVELLER          │
   │ "Alexa, a hotel in │
   │  Naples with pool" │
   └─────────┬──────────┘
             │
             ▼
   ┌────────────────────┐
   │ INTENT RECOGNITION │
   │ → commercial +     │
   │   location + limit │
   └─────────┬──────────┘
             │
             ▼
   ┌────────────────────┐
   │ KNOWLEDGE GRAPH    │
   │ Bing / Google      │
   │ → looks for Hotel  │
   │   schema, services │
   └─────────┬──────────┘
             │
             ▼
   ┌────────────────────┐
   │ FEATURED SNIPPET   │
   │ → FAQ page with a  │
   │   40–60 word answer│
   └─────────┬──────────┘
             │
             ▼
   ┌────────────────────┐
   │ SINGLE ANSWER      │
   │ → read aloud       │
   │                    │
   └─────────┬──────────┘
             │
             ▼
   ┌────────────────────┐
   │ CONVERSION         │
   │ "Shall I book?"    │
   │ → direct booking   │
   └────────────────────┘

Six mistakes that keep you out of voice results

MistakeConsequenceThe fix
No schema markupInvisible to voiceImplement Hotel, LocalBusiness and FAQ
Inconsistent name, address and phoneLoss of algorithmic trustAlign them everywhere
A slow site (LCP over 3s)Excluded from featured snippetsOptimise images, lazy loading, a CDN
Headings written as marketing copyNo match with real queriesRewrite as question and answer
An incomplete or unverified Business ProfileHalves your chances on "near me"Verify and complete it fully
Malformed schema (JSON-LD errors)Google penalises youValidate with the Rich Results Test

A real case: an 18-room boutique hotel in central Naples

A four-star boutique hotel in the historic centre of Naples, 18 rooms, mainly international guests from the US, UK and German-speaking Europe. Starting point (January 2025):

  • A modern site, but with no schema markup
  • No FAQ sections
  • Business Profile 60% complete, no posts
  • Page speed: LCP 4.1s, INP 380ms
  • Direct bookings from the site: 38 a month
  • Voice-attributed traffic: 0.4% of the total

What we did in 90 days

  1. A complete voice SEO audit across 47 checkpoints, with a prioritised report
  2. Schema implementation: Hotel, LocalBusiness, FAQPage and Review, validated with the Rich Results Test
  3. FAQs added across all 14 main pages — 84 questions and answers, written around spoken long-tail queries
  4. Headings rewritten as questions, with a short answer beneath
  5. Twelve location-intent pages ("Getting here from the port", "Hotels near the cathedral", "What to do in the Decumani in a day")
  6. Page speed work: WebP images, lazy loading, preloaded fonts, a CDN — LCP down to 1.8s
  7. Business Profile to 100%: 60 new photographs, a 750-character description, a Q&A section with 25 questions
  8. NAP audit across 47 directories — TripAdvisor, OTAs, social, Apple Maps, Bing Places — with corrections

Results after six months

KPIBefore (Jan 2025)After (Jul 2025)Change
Total organic traffic5,200/month9,840/month+89%
Voice-attributed traffic0.4%17.2%+4,200%
Featured snippets won234+1,600%
Number one positions on spoken long-tail341+1,266%
Page speed (LCP)4.1s1.8s−56%
Direct bookings per month3897+155%
Average value of a direct booking€198€241+22%
OTA commission savedbaseline~€11,400/month+€11,400
"I thought voice search was something for American geeks. Then we saw that 17% of our traffic came from American guests saying 'Hey Google' in the car from the airport. Since we became the answer that gets read out for queries like 'boutique hotel near Naples cathedral', direct bookings have doubled. And every direct booking is 18% of OTA commission we do not pay." — Marketing manager, four-star boutique hotel in Naples (18 rooms)

A 90-day roadmap

Month 1 — Technical foundations

  1. Full audit: schema, FAQs, page speed, Business Profile, NAP
  2. Implement Hotel, LocalBusiness and Review schema
  3. Validate with the Rich Results Test, aiming for zero errors
  4. Page speed work, targeting LCP under 2.5s
  5. NAP audit and corrections across every directory

Month 2 — Voice-ready content

  1. FAQs on every page — 60 to 100 questions for an average hotel
  2. FAQPage schema wherever there are FAQs
  3. Rewrite headings so they can be answered
  4. Build 8 to 15 location-intent pages
  5. Complete the Business Profile with photos, description and Q&A

Month 3 — Tracking and tuning

  1. Set up voice-attributed tracking in your analytics
  2. Monitor which featured snippets you win
  3. A/B test the wording of FAQ answers
  4. Weekly Business Profile posts
  5. Monthly KPI reporting and tuning
⚠️ One warning: malformed schema markup is worse than none. Google detects the JSON-LD error and applies an algorithmic penalty that keeps you out of featured snippets for weeks. A documented case: a hotel added Review schema with aggregateRating but no "itemReviewed" field — Google issued a manual action and the property vanished from results for 22 days. Always validate with the Rich Results Test before publishing.

Related reading

To build a rounded digital strategy for your hotel, read also:

  • Local SEO for hotels: reaching Google's top three in 90 days — the local SEO foundations everything else rests on
  • AI chatbots for hotels: your 24/7 digital front desk — how conversational AI completes the voice experience
  • AI dynamic pricing for hotels — why direct bookings from voice are the highest-margin channel to optimise

In closing: the voice is the new screen

By 2027, one hotel booking in two in Italy will begin with a sentence spoken to a smart speaker, to a phone in hands-free mode, or to a car assistant. This is not a marketing forecast: it is a hardware and behavioural shift already under way that will not stop.

Whoever optimises for voice now builds an advantage that compounds: featured snippets won today will be hard for latecomers to take. Whoever waits until 2027 will find a saturated market and acquisition costs twice as high.

The good news: voice SEO does not need an enormous budget. It needs method, clean schema markup, content in question-and-answer form, and the patience to give it 90 days. The return, in OTA commission saved and direct bookings won, pays back in under six months.

item.title: Direct Bookings: Cutting OTA Commission and Raising Margins by 40%
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
On every €800 booking, Booking.com keeps €144. It is not a one-off fee: it is the 18% that leaves every time a guest clicks "Book" on a portal instead of on your own site. Across 200 bookings a year that is €28,800 handed to an intermediary who, in the meantime, also keeps your customer's email address. The question is no longer whether to reduce your dependence on them, but how much you are losing every month you put the decision off.

What an OTA booking really costs — and it is not just the commission

When a hotel manager works out the cost of Booking.com or Expedia, they stop at the contract percentage: 15%, 17%, 18% if you are in a visibility programme. That is the number on the invoice, so it is the only one that reaches the budget. And it is the least painful part of the bill.

1. The commission is the tip of the iceberg

Layered on top of the declared 18% are invisible costs: the preferred partner programme that adds three to five percentage points to stay visible, sponsored campaigns inside the portal, cancellation penalties handled under the OTA's rules rather than yours. Many Campania properties we analyse pay a real distribution cost of 21–24%, not the 15% they believe.

2. The customer is not yours, it is theirs

Every OTA booking arrives with a masked email address (@guest.booking.com) that stops working a few weeks after check-out. No real phone number, no marketing consent, no preferences. You have hosted someone for four nights and at the end of the stay you cannot write to them at all: that customer lives in a database in Amsterdam, not in yours.

3. No remarketing means no recurring return

A guest acquired directly enters a cycle that continues: a pre-stay email for upselling, a review request, an offer when the season reopens, a loyalty code. A guest acquired through an OTA reaches a dead end. If they return, they return through Booking, and you pay commission a second time on a customer you had already won.

Item (average three-night stay) Via an OTA Direct
Gross room revenue€744 (ADR €248)€813 (ADR €271)
Portal commission (17.5%)−€130€0
Acquisition cost (metasearch, ads, booking engine)€0−€41
Cost of the exclusive perks offered€0−€18
Immediate net margin€614€754
Usable contact dataNo (masked email)Yes, owned and profiled

Cumulative margin over 24 months€651€919 (+41%)

📌 The number that actually matters
Do not look at the margin on a single booking: look at the margin on an acquired guest over 24 months. That is where the direct channel pulls more than 40 percentage points ahead, because re-acquiring a customer already in your database costs around €4, against the €130 of commission you pay a portal every single time.

The billboard paradox: OTAs are useful, just not as your only channel

Something many consultants avoid saying: Booking.com is not the enemy. It is the largest engine of travel discovery in the world, and for a 30-room property in Positano or on Ischia it is a shop window no marketing budget could replicate.

The phenomenon is called the billboard effect: the traveller discovers the property on a portal, then searches the hotel's name on Google and decides elsewhere. Serious estimates put it at 45–55% of users who, having seen a property on an OTA, visit the official site before booking. If that site is slow, if the booking engine takes five steps, if the price is identical to the portal's, the user goes back to the OTA and you pay commission on a customer who had already been delivered to you.

The aim is not to eliminate the portals: it is to shift the balance. A healthy mix for an independent property in Campania is 60% direct and owned channels, 40% OTAs and intermediaries. Those who reach 100% direct almost always lose volume and occupancy; those who stay below 15% direct are financing a competitor's growth.

The six pillars of a book-direct strategy that works

1. A fast, mobile-first booking engine: fewer than three clicks

Sixty-eight per cent of traffic to Campania hotel sites comes from phones, yet mobile conversion averages a third of desktop. The reason is almost always the same: booking engines designed in 2016, with calendars that do not open properly on touch and forms with seven fields. The working rule is blunt but effective: from the home page to the payment page there should be at most three clicks, and the whole thing should load in under three seconds on 4G.

2. A visible best rate guarantee, not one buried in the footer

If the guest does not know your site has the best rate, they will go and check on Booking and stay there. The "best price guaranteed" badge belongs above the fold, next to the booking button, worded plainly: "Book here for the lowest price. Find it cheaper elsewhere and we will refund the difference." It costs nothing and moves conversion by 8 to 14 percentage points.

3. Exclusive perks on direct: change the game, not the price

Competing on price with an OTA is a war you lose. Competing on perceived value is one you win at almost no cost. Late check-out, an upgrade, breakfast included, a discounted transfer from the port: these cost you a few euros and the guest values them at tens.

4. Google Hotel Ads and metasearch: catch the people already looking for you

When someone searches your hotel's name on Google, the side panel shows the portals' rates. If you are not in that panel with your own rate, you are handing Booking the click on your own brand. Google Hotel Ads works on commission — typically 10–12%, often less on a cost-per-click basis — and remains considerably cheaper than an OTA, with the advantage that the customer lands on your booking engine and the data stays yours.

5. Email marketing to your own database

A list of 5,000 profiled contacts is worth, for a 40-room property, between €40,000 and €70,000 of direct revenue a year. It needs minimal segmentation — past guests, people who only enquired, high-season against low-season stayers — and three well-made campaigns a year: season opening, a targeted last-minute offer, a holiday promotion.

6. A light loyalty scheme, not a points card

Forget complicated systems. What works far better is one simple rule you can state in a line: "Anyone who has stayed with us always books at 10% off on the official site, for life." It costs a tenth of the margin but turns an occasional customer into a recurring one, and above all it is the lever that moves the rebooking from the portal to your own channel.

💡 The golden rule of perks
The perk has to be impossible to get on the portal and immediately understandable. "10% off" is weak and erodes your margin. "Late check-out until 2pm and breakfast included, only when you book here" is strong, costs less, and does not start a price war with the OTA.

Rate parity: what the contract really says, and what Italian law says

This is every hotelier's first fear: "If I put a lower price on my own site, Booking will penalise me or close my account." It is a widespread belief and, in Italy, legally unfounded.

📌 In Italy, strict parity clauses have been void since 2017
Italy's annual competition law (Law 124/2017, article 1, paragraph 166) declared null any contractual clause preventing an accommodation business from offering better prices and booking conditions on its own direct channels than on intermediation platforms. In practice: you may legally sell for less on your own site. The EU Platform-to-Business Regulation and the Digital Markets Act have reinforced the same direction.

That said, undercutting aggressively and publicly is rarely the best strategy, because it triggers an algorithmic reaction in the portal's ranking. The intelligent route is the one the chains have used for years: matched public rate, differentiated value. The same visible price, but on direct you add breakfast, late check-out, a more flexible cancellation. And for closed rates — promotional codes, newsletter-only rates, offers for past guests — you have complete freedom, because those are not public prices.

Eight mistakes that kill direct bookings

Mistake Measured impact The fix
A site that loads in over three seconds−32% conversion for each second beyond the thresholdWebP images, a CDN, dedicated hosting
A booking engine with five or more steps−54% funnel completionReduce to three: dates → room → payment
An experience that is not mobile-firstMobile conversion at a third of desktopMobile-first redesign, touch-friendly calendar

No mention of the best rateThe user opens the portal to checkA best rate guarantee badge next to the call to action
A booking engine only in ItalianUp to −40% on international marketsReal multilingual support: English, German, French
No email capture before bookingA static database, no remarketingAn exit-intent pop-up with a concrete offer
No abandoned-cart recoveryAbout 78% leave before payingAutomatic emails at one hour and 24 hours

A real case: a 45-room four-star on the Amalfi Coast

A seasonal property open 230 days a year, heavily dependent on Booking.com and Expedia, with a website built in 2019 and never touched since, and a booking engine thrown in "free" with the property management system. Starting point: 12% direct bookings, the rest split between portals (71%) and tour operators or groups (17%).

What changed over 14 months: a new mobile-first site with a three-step booking engine, Google Hotel Ads on the brand, a prominent best rate guarantee, a package of exclusive direct perks, automated pre- and post-stay emails, and a 10%-for-life loyalty scheme for past guests.

KPI Before After 14 months Change
Share of direct bookings12%34%+22 points
OTA commission paid (year)€204,000€148,500−€55,500
ADR, direct channel€244€271+11%
ADR, OTA channel€248€251+1%
Technology and direct advertising cost€6,000€31,000+€25,000

Profiled email database1,240 contacts6,850 contacts+452%
Returning guests on the direct channel4%19%+15 points
Site conversion rate0.9%3.4%+278%

The most underrated figure is the last one. Traffic to the site grew only 26%, but direct revenue nearly tripled. The problem was never getting people to the site: it was not losing them once they arrived.

For years I thought commission was a fixed cost of the trade, like linen or electricity. When we saw the first monthly report with 34 direct bookings instead of 11, I realised I had been paying €200,000 a year for not having a website that worked. What surprised me most was not the saving: it was discovering that guests who book directly spend more in the restaurant and come back.

— General manager, 45-room four-star hotel, Amalfi Coast

The first 90 days

Days 1–30: measure, and fix the foundations

Before spending a euro on advertising you need to know where you stand. Calculate the real distribution cost channel by channel, measure site speed on mobile with PageSpeed Insights, count how many clicks it genuinely takes to book. Install event tracking on the booking engine: without data on where people drop out, every later optimisation is guesswork. In parallel, put the best rate guarantee and a starting price on the home page — two changes that take hours and produce results immediately.

Days 31–60: make the direct channel competitive

This is conversion work. A three-step booking engine, a calendar usable on a phone, multiple languages if you serve international markets. Define and publish the package of exclusive perks, stating it on every room page. Switch on Google Hotel Ads at least for brand queries: it is the fastest way to stop paying commission on people already searching for you by name. Start collecting emails properly, at booking and at check-in.

Days 61–90: build the recurring return

Automate the email cycle: confirmation, pre-stay with upselling, post-stay with a review request and a loyalty code. Switch on abandoned-cart recovery. Launch the loyalty scheme to the database you already have, however small. From here it is monthly maintenance: watch the channel mix, test the perks, move budget from OTA inventory towards direct without sudden movements.

⚠️ Do not cut the OTAs abruptly
The most expensive mistake we see is the hotelier who, encouraged by early results, drastically reduces portal inventory or closes a channel overnight. The outcome is almost always the same: the billboard effect collapses, you vanish from discovery searches, occupancy falls 10 to 15 points, and it takes two seasons to recover the lost ranking. Reducing intermediation is a progression, not a switch. Cut your dependence by growing direct, not by cutting indirect.

  • Local SEO for hotels: reaching the top of Google — why organic traffic on your name and on destination queries is the free fuel of the direct channel.
  • AI dynamic pricing: how to raise RevPAR — how to make dynamic pricing and channel mix work together to maximise margin, not just occupancy.

In closing: direct is an asset, an OTA is a channel

The fundamental difference is this. A euro spent advertising on a portal produces a booking and ends there. A euro spent on the direct channel produces a booking, a contact, a piece of data, a relationship and — in 22% of cases — a second booking at almost no cost. The first is an expense; the second is an investment that accumulates season after season.

You do not have to change everything in a month. You have to stop treating 18% as an unavoidable cost and start treating it as what it is: the largest and most addressable line in your profit and loss.

item.title: Online Reviews for Hotels: Going From 8.1 to 9.0 on Booking in Six Months
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every tenth of a point on your Booking score is worth an average of 2.3% of RevPAR. Going from 8.1 to 9.0 is nine tenths: roughly 20% more revenue from the same rooms in the same season. No advertising spend returns as much. Yet 71% of Italian properties never reply to negative reviews, and let the unhappy guest write the only version of the story the next traveller will read.

Reputation is not an image question: it is a pricing lever. The score decides where you appear, whether you survive the filter the user applies before even looking at the photographs, and how much you can charge for the same room.

Why the score matters more than you think

Three separate mechanisms stack up, and almost no hotelier keeps them apart.

1. The ranking algorithm treats it as a strong signal

Booking.com orders results by combining commission, conversion, availability, rate and quality. The score enters twice: as an absolute value and as freshness — how many reviews you have had in the past twelve months. Two identical properties at the same price do not appear in the same position if one has 8.2 from 30 reviews and the other 8.9 from 210.

2. The "8+" filter cuts out anyone below it

Sixty-two per cent of users set a minimum score before scrolling, and almost always the value they pick is 8+ ("Very good"). Below that threshold you are not competing badly: you are not appearing. The next threshold, decisive in high-spending northern European markets, is 9+.

3. The score is the price you can afford to charge

This is the point that matters most. At the same category and location, a guest will accept 10–15% more if your score is visibly better than your competitors'. Reputation is what lets you leave the price war without losing occupancy.

Booking score Label Sustainable ADR against the local average Effect on positioning
7.0 – 7.9Good−10% / −18%Excluded by the 8+ filter; you compete on price alone
8.0 – 8.4Very goodIn line with the averageYou pass the filter, but stay on page two
8.5 – 8.9Very good+4% / +8%Page one on low-pressure dates
9.0 – 9.3Excellent+12% / +18%Consistently page one; you pass the 9+ filter
9.4 +Exceptional+20% / +28%Top five locally, badges and editorial visibility

The correct reading is not "going up is good": it is that the steps are not linear. Moving from 7.9 to 8.0, or from 8.9 to 9.0, is worth far more than any other tenth, because it crosses a filter threshold. If you are at 8.8, the two tenths you are missing are the most profitable investment in front of you.

Anatomy of the score: six sub-categories, and which ones move the needle

Booking calculates the score as an average of six areas. They look equivalent, but they are not in terms of what you can change: some are entirely in your hands, others not at all.

Sub-category How much you control it Cost to improve Real priority
CleanlinessCompletelyOrganisational, not financialHighest
StaffCompletelyTraining, two or three hours a monthHighest
ComfortLargelyModerate (mattresses, soundproofing)High
FacilitiesPartlyModerate to highMedium
Value for moneyIndirectlyRises on its own as the others doMedium
LocationNot at allCannot be changedLow

Cleanliness and staff move the average more than anything else, for two reasons: they are what guests mention in the free text — and the text is what the next traveller reads — and they need process, not investment. A signed housekeeping checklist, a spot check on three rooms a day and a standard welcome line produce more points than a €40,000 refurbishment.

📌 Location is the trap. It is the item hoteliers cite most often to explain a low score — "we are outside the centre" — and the only one you can do nothing about. If the location is awkward, do not apologise for it: state it precisely in your listing. Guests punish unmet expectations, not distance.

The volume rule: 200 reviews at 8.7 beat 40 at 9.2

This is the most counter-intuitive idea in reputation management, and the one that loses the most money. A high score built on few judgements is worth less than a slightly lower one built on many.

  • Perceived trust. A user mentally discounts a 9.2 from 40 reviews: they know four friends and a relative would do it. An 8.7 from 200 is statistically credible.
  • Stability. With 40 reviews, a single score of 4 drags you down 0.13 points; with 200 the same review weighs 0.03. Volume is your insurance against the impossible guest.
  • Algorithmic freshness. The platforms weight recent reviews more heavily. Collecting 15 a month tells the ranking you are alive; sitting at three a year, as far as the algorithm is concerned, you might be closed.

Hence the order of operations: raise the volume first, then work on the average. Doing it the other way round means chasing tenths while the denominator stays too small for anything to show.

Raising the volume without breaking the platforms' rules

The rule you cannot work around: you may not offer anything in exchange for a review, nor pick who to ask based on how happy you think they are. You may ask everyone, at the right moment and on the right channel — and that is where almost everyone goes wrong.

The timing

The useful window is 12 to 36 hours after check-out. Earlier, the guest is travelling; later, the memory blurs and the response rate collapses. Asking during the stay is the classic mistake: it is a judgement on an incomplete experience.

The channel

On Booking the invitation comes from the platform: what you control is reminding the guest at check-out that they will receive it. Ten seconds at the desk doubles the completion rate. On Google and TripAdvisor you generate the request yourself, with a direct link to the review form, never to the profile home page.

QR codes in the room and at the desk

A QR code on a card in the room and one at the desk are the highest-yield channel for Google, and cost twenty euros to print. The wording must be neutral — "Tell us how it went" — never "Leave us five stars", which breaches the platforms' guidelines and can cost you the profile.

The automated post-stay email

It is the only tool that scales. A single email 24 hours after check-out, with the guest's name and one link, takes the review rate from 6–8% to 15–22% of departures. No reminders: whoever does not answer the first will not answer the third.

   CHECK-OUT (hour 0)

     ▼                 ▼          ▼

The private feedback branch is not a filter: the public review always remains possible. It is routing — a solvable complaint gets solved before it becomes permanent, and the guest who receives the manager's call often writes anyway, but writes something different.

What is your current score costing you?

We analyse your reviews from the past twelve months free of charge, identify the three recurring problems costing you tenths of a point, and tell you how much ADR you are leaving on the table. Answer within 48 hours.

Request the free analysis Message us on WhatsApp

Replying to a negative review: the five-step formula

One premise changes everything: the reply is not written for the person who complained. It is written for the 300 travellers who will read that exchange while deciding whether to book with you.

  1. Thank them, briefly. One line, no corporate preamble.
  2. Acknowledge the specific fact. Name the problem in their words: the reader has to see that you understood.
  3. Explain without over-apologising. A sentence of context, not a defence. Excessive apology sounds as insincere as a defence.
  4. State a concrete action. What has changed, with a verifiable detail. This is the part that convinces the outside reader.
  5. Move the rest to private. A direct contact, away from the shop window.
❌ The wrong reply ✅ The right reply
"Dear guest, we are very sorry for the inconvenience. Your opinion is extremely important to us. We assure you that our standards are always of the highest level and that the noise you mention is entirely exceptional, not least because no other customer has ever complained. We apologise again and hope to welcome you back soon." "Thank you for telling us, Marta.
The roadworks noise was real, on the mornings of the 12th and 13th, and on the street-side rooms it was heavy.
The works finished on 20 March, and from this week rooms 204–208 are the last to be allocated for short stays.
If you decide to come back, write to me: I'll keep a courtyard-side room for you.
Luca, manager"

Four differences are measurable: the second uses the name, cites verifiable dates, contains a dated action and is signed by a real person. The first denies the problem and closes with a formula already seen on two hundred identical listings.

Type of negative review Mistake to avoid What to say instead
NoiseSaying nobody else complainedConfirm it, give the date the disruption ended, offer the quiet side
CleanlinessReplying that standards are "extremely high"A clear, short apology; name the check you introduced and from when
Breakfast or foodDefending the supplier or the menuThank them and name the change already made to the offering
Rude staffDisputing the guest's accountTake responsibility, mention the training, sign with the manager's name
Too expensiveJustifying the rate line by lineAcknowledge the perception, list in one line what is included, invite them to book direct
Expectations not metReplying "it was all in the listing"Admit the communication was not clear, say what you have corrected in the listing

⚠️ Three mistakes that cost more than the reviews themselves.
Never ask for a review to be removed simply because it is negative: the platforms remove only what breaks their policies — abuse, personal data, false statements, blackmail — and repeated spurious requests flag your profile. Never reply in the heat of the moment: leave twenty-four hours and have a second person read it. Never copy and paste the same reply: anyone reading three identical replies in a row works out in three seconds that nobody read anything, and the damage exceeds that of the original reviews.

A real case: a 28-room three-star in central Naples

A property open year-round near Piazza Bellini, 55% international leisure and 45% domestic business. Starting point: 8.1 on Booking, 340 historical reviews but only nine new ones a month, and no public replies to negatives for two years.

Six months of changes, none of them structural: a housekeeping checklist signed by the head housekeeper, a check on three rooms every morning, a standard line at check-out, QR codes in the room and at the desk for Google, a post-stay email at 24 hours, and a reply to every review within 48 hours.

KPI Before After 6 months Change
Booking score8.19.0+0.9 points
New reviews per month931+244%
Review response rate4%100%+96 points
Cleanliness sub-score7.89.1+1.3
Staff sub-score8.69.4+0.8
Average ADR€96€114+18.7%
Booking ranking position (city centre)#41#12+29 places
Average occupancy68%79%+11 points
Total Google reviews112287+156%

The arithmetic is simple: across 28 rooms, €18 more ADR and 11 points of occupancy are worth roughly €78,000 of extra room revenue in a year. The direct cost was €40 to print the QR codes. The rest was time: thirty minutes a week.

I thought raising the score meant redoing the bathrooms. It was enough to stop pretending the complaints did not exist. After three months guests started writing to us quoting the replies themselves: "I chose you because I saw how you answer."

— Owner, 28-room three-star hotel, central Naples

The weekly routine: thirty minutes is enough

Reputation is not managed in projects, it is managed by rhythm. A fixed block in the diary, always the same day, returns more than any one-off initiative.

  • 15 minutes — the replies. Every review from the week: negatives first, positives with two lines citing a detail of the stay. None left beyond 48 hours.
  • 10 minutes — the count. On one sheet: Booking score, Google score, new reviews, and the words that recur in the negative texts. Always in the same place.
  • 5 minutes — the briefing. One thing to fix this week, told to whoever has to do it. One, not five: the long list never gets done.
  • Every quarter, 60 minutes — the review. How the six sub-scores are trending, the monthly volume, and a check that your listing and photographs match reality.

💡 Reviews are your free operational roadmap. They are continuous consultancy written by people who paid to use your product. The complaints that repeat are your to-do list, already sorted by how often they appear. If the word "breakfast" comes up eleven times in a negative tone over three months, that is not an opinion: it is a job you are putting off. Extract the recurring themes every quarter and treat them as work orders, not feedback.

item.title: Email Marketing for Hotels: Pre-Stay, Post-Stay and Recovering Abandoned Bookings
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-eight per cent of people who start a booking on your site abandon it before confirming. A single automatic email sent 45 minutes after they leave recovers between 12% and 18% of them. Across 300 abandonments a year that is 40 extra bookings: direct, commission-free, and without a cent spent on advertising. Yet most hotels in Campania do not have a single sequence running.

Email marketing for hotels is not "sending a Christmas newsletter". It is a system of three automatic sequences working on the database you already own: people who visited the booking engine and did not finish, people who booked and have not arrived yet, and people who have just left. Three moments, three different commercial objectives, all measurable in euros.

Why email beats every other channel for a hotel

The difference is not aesthetic preference, it is economic structure. On Meta and Google you rent access to an audience: stop paying and the traffic disappears. With email you own the list. Every address collected is an asset that keeps producing revenue for years at almost no marginal cost.

The second point is commission. A recovered booking on a €180-a-night room for three nights is €540 of full revenue. The same booking arriving from an OTA at 18% leaves you €443. The difference, €97, is the margin that funds ten years of your email tool subscription.

Channel Cost per booking Who owns the audience Average return
Email marketing €1.50 – €4 Yours, a database you own €36 per €1 spent
Meta Ads €18 – €45 Rented €4 – €7 per €1
Google Ads, brand €8 – €22 Rented €6 – €12 per €1
OTAs (Booking, Expedia) 15% – 22% of the stay The OTA's — you never see the customer Net revenue −18%

📌 The €36 return for every euro invested is the travel and hospitality sector average. Even halving it to be cautious, it remains the highest-yielding channel available to an independent property.

The three sequences every property needs

You do not need twenty automations. You need three, built well and left to run. Each catches a different moment in the guest's life cycle and has a distinct commercial objective.

  • Sequence 1 — Abandoned booking recovery. Objective: convert someone who has already been on the booking engine. The most profitable of all, because it works on warm, qualified demand.
  • Sequence 2 — Pre-stay. Objective: raise the average spend with upselling and ancillaries before arrival, and reduce enquiries to the front desk.
  • Sequence 3 — Post-stay. Objective: collect reviews and turn the guest into a returner, the customer who costs nothing to acquire.

Sequence 1 — Recovering the abandoned booking

Someone who reaches the payment page and does not confirm is not browsing: they have already chosen dates, room and rate. They stopped for a mundane reason — a phone call, a doubt about cancellation, the urge to compare the price on Booking. Three emails across 72 hours recover a substantial share of these people.

Email 1 — 45 minutes after abandonment

The most important of the whole architecture. It should be helpful, not commercial: no discount, no pressure. Summarise the dates, room and price, and offer a link back to the basket already filled in. A plain subject line: "Your room for 14–17 June is still available". Conversion here runs at 12–18%.

Email 2 — 24 hours later

Change the lever: from logistical convenience to reassurance. Free cancellation, best price guaranteed on the official site, a direct WhatsApp contact with reception. This is where the honest comparison with the OTA belongs: the same price, but with priority upgrade and late check-out included where available. Expected conversion: 5–8%.

Email 3 — 72 hours later

The last call, with real scarcity, not invented: how many rooms remain for those dates. Only here, and only if the margin allows, can you introduce a light incentive — breakfast included, or 5% off — never an aggressive discount that erodes rate parity. Conversion: 3–5%.

Timing Subject Key content Call to action Expected conversion
45 minutes Your room for [dates] is still available Booking summary, room photograph, no discount Complete your booking 12% – 18%
24 hours One question before you decide Free cancellation, best price, reception's WhatsApp Pick up where you left off 5% – 8%
72 hours [N] rooms left for [dates] Real availability, breakfast included if offered Lock in the rate 3% – 5%

⚠️ The recovery sequence only works if the booking engine captures the email before the payment step. If your engine asks for the address only at the last stage, you are losing the data of precisely the people who abandon. That is the first thing to check, before even choosing a tool.

Sequence 2 — Pre-stay: upselling and preparing the stay

On average 45 days pass between confirmation and arrival. In that window the guest is in the most favourable emotional state: they have already made the hard decision and are now imagining the holiday. It is the point of highest willingness to spend in the whole cycle, and most hotels leave it completely empty.

Seven days before — the experience email

Not a service email but a curated catalogue: airport transfer, sea-view upgrade, a tour of Pompeii or Capri, dinner on the terrace. Present it as "get your stay ready", not as a sale. Typical overall take-up: 18–25% of guests buy at least one extra.

Two days before — logistics and one last offer

Check-in times, how to get there, parking, the weather forecast. At the end, just two high-converting offers: transfer and late check-out. The simplification is deliberate — two days from departure, the guest has no appetite for choosing between ten options.

Arrival day — the welcome message

The name of the person on reception, a direct WhatsApp number, an expected arrival time to confirm with one click. No selling. This email cuts phone calls to the front desk and opens the channel you will use throughout the stay.

Extra Suggested price Expected take-up Margin When to send
Transfer from Naples airport €85 – €110 each way 22% 25% – 30% 7 and 2 days before
Sea-view room upgrade €35 – €60 a night 12% 85% – 95% 7 days before
Late check-out (3pm) €40 – €70 15% 90% – 100% 2 days before
Dinner on the terrace (two people) €90 – €140 9% 60% – 65% 7 days before
Pompeii tour / Capri by boat €120 – €250 11% 15% – 20% (commission) 7 days before

The detail that changes the numbers: upgrades and late check-out carry almost full margin because they sell capacity that would otherwise go unsold. Those are the first two to switch on, always.

The complete timeline

  ABANDONMENT              BOOKING                    STAY                 AFTER
      │                       │                        │                    │
  ┌───┴────┐             ┌────┴─────┐             ┌────┴────┐         ┌─────┴──────┐
  │ SEQ. 1 │             │  SEQ. 2  │             │ CHECK-IN│         │   SEQ. 3   │
  │RECOVERY│             │ PRE-STAY │             │         │         │ POST-STAY  │
  └───┬────┘             └────┬─────┘             └────┬────┘         └─────┬──────┘
      │                       │                        │                    │
   +45 min  ──▶ confirmed?    │                        │                +24 h  ──▶ review
      │  no                   │                        │                    │
   +24 h   ──▶ confirmed?  −7 days ──▶ experiences     │                +7 days ──▶ content +
      │  no                   │        and upgrades     │                    │      referral code
   +72 h   ──▶ last call   −2 days ──▶ logistics +     │                    │
      │                       │        transfer         │                +3 months ──▶ return
      X  lost              day 0 ──▶ welcome  ─────────┘                    │          offer
                                                                             │
                                                                        RETURNING GUEST
                                                                      (zero acquisition cost)

How many bookings are you losing each month?

We analyse your booking engine free of charge and tell you how many abandonments it produces, what they are worth in euros, and which sequences to switch on first. No commitment, answer within 48 hours.

Request the free analysis Message us on WhatsApp

Sequence 3 — Post-stay: reviews and loyalty

A guest who has just left has the most vivid memory and the highest willingness to engage. Every day that passes without contacting them loses you both the review and the chance of a return.

24 hours after — the review request

A personal thank you and one link. The rule that doubles results: if the stay had known problems, the first email asks for private feedback; the public link to Google or TripAdvisor goes only to those who respond positively. This is not filtering reviews, it is routing the conversation to the right place. The response rate typically goes from 6–8% to 15–22%.

Seven days after — content and referral

No direct selling. Your best photographs, a guide to the places the guest did not have time to see, and a referral code to pass to friends and family. Its job is to stay in mind during the week they tell everyone about the holiday.

Three months after — the seasonal return offer

Here you sell. An offer built around the opposite season to their stay — someone who came in August receives a proposal for the spring break, with a "returning guest" rate and a limited booking window. Typical conversion 4–7%, at zero acquisition cost.

The minimum segmentation that actually works

You do not need twenty segments. Four are enough, built from data your PMS already holds:

  • Business against leisure. Inferable from length of stay and days of the week. Business guests get late check-out and transfers; leisure guests get experiences and dinners. Sending the wrong email to the wrong segment is the fastest way to be ignored.
  • First stay against returning. You do not explain to a returning guest where the property is: you acknowledge their status and give them a dedicated rate.
  • Nationality and language. At an Amalfi Coast hotel the mix is typically 40–60% international. A pre-stay sequence in English converts nearly twice as well as the same one in Italian for English-speaking guests.
  • Season of stay. Determines what to offer in the three-month email and over what window.

💡 If time is short, start with language and first-stay against returning alone. They capture 80% of the relevance gain for 20% of the configuration work.

The tools, and what they really cost

Tool Indicative cost per year Strength When it fits
Brevo (formerly Sendinblue) €300 – €700 Complete automation, priced per send The standard for 20–80 room hotels in Italy
Mailchimp €400 – €1,100 Simplicity, ready-made templates Newsletters only, few automations
Klaviyo €900 – €2,400 Advanced segmentation and revenue tracking Groups with several properties and high volume
ActiveCampaign €700 – €1,800 Built-in CRM, conditional logic Anyone also running events and meetings
The email module in your PMS or booking engine €0 – €400 Data already connected, no integration work A starting point if it is already in your subscription

The criterion is not richness of features but integration: a tool that talks natively to your booking engine is worth more than a more powerful one that needs a fragile connector. Always check, before signing, that an integration with your engine exists.

⚠️ GDPR — the distinction you need to know. Operational pre-stay and post-stay emails (confirmation, logistics, check-in) are transactional: the legal basis is performance of the contract and they do not require marketing consent. Commercial offers, the newsletter and the three-month return email are promotional and require explicit consent, collected with an unticked checkbox, preferably double opt-in, with proof of collection retained and an unsubscribe link in every send. Mixing the two in the same automation is the mistake that exposes you to a penalty: keep them on separate lists and flows.

A real case: a 52-room four-star in Sorrento

A seasonal property open from March to November, 52 rooms, average ADR €195, heavily dependent on the OTAs (72% of sales). No email automation at all: just a newsletter sent by hand three times a year. The three sequences were implemented in 60 days, with Brevo connected to the existing booking engine.

KPI (12 months) Before After Value generated
Bookings recovered from abandonment 0 47 €21,150
Pre-stay upsell revenue €2,400 (at the desk) €13,800 €11,400
Reviews collected (% of departures) 7% 21% +142 reviews
Guest return rate 6% 11% €5,900
Total — — €38,450

Tool cost for the year: €540. The net return is roughly seventy times the spend, before counting what 142 extra reviews are worth to positioning on the OTAs and on Google.

The surprise was not the upselling, which we expected. It was the 45-minute email: 47 bookings in a year that we simply believed lost, without spending another euro on advertising. What convinced me is that it worked in November too, with the property half empty.

— Revenue manager, 52-room four-star hotel, Sorrento

Setting it up in 30 days

Week 1 — Foundations. Check that the booking engine captures the email before payment. Choose the tool and connect it. Configure domain authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC): without it half your emails land in spam and everything else is pointless.

Week 2 — Sequence 1. Write and switch on the three abandonment recovery emails. This is the sequence with the fastest return: it goes first and starts producing within days.

Week 3 — Sequence 2. Build the upsell catalogue with prices and margins defined, set up the three pre-stay emails and how extras are paid for. Translate it all into English.

Week 4 — Sequence 3 and measurement. Switch on the post-stay emails, set the minimum segmentation, configure revenue attribution by email, and fix a monthly review of the numbers.

💡 If you implement one thing from this article, implement the 45-minute abandonment email. It is the single highest-return automation available to a property: a few hours of setup, no discounting, no effect on rate parity, and it works on customers who had already chosen you. Everything else can wait a month.

Related reading

  • Increasing direct bookings: the guide to reducing intermediation — email is one pillar, but it belongs inside a wider strategy for cutting OTA dependence.
  • Managing online reviews on Booking and TripAdvisor — what to do with the 142 extra reviews the post-stay sequence brings you.
  • AI dynamic pricing: how to raise RevPAR — why the rates you quote in recovery emails have to be consistent with your pricing strategy.

In closing

Email marketing for hotels is not a creative channel, it is an industrial one: three sequences, one configuration done properly, and a flow of revenue that keeps turning while you do something else. The €38,000 in the Sorrento case did not come from a brilliant idea, but from covering three moments that had previously been empty.

The cost of doing nothing is silent, which is what makes it dangerous: the abandonments you do not recover appear in no report, the upsells you do not offer show up nowhere, and the guests who do not return never tell you why.
