item.title: Metasearch for Hotels: Google Hotel Ads, Trivago and TripAdvisor
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
When a customer searches your hotel's name on Google, the first thing they see is not your website: it is a box of rates. If Booking is in there at €140 and your official site is not, you have just paid 18% commission on a customer who was already looking for you by name. That is not a customer the OTA brought you: it is a customer the OTA intercepted in the last metre. Metasearch exists to take that metre back.

It is the highest-returning form of advertising available to an independent property, because it does not buy cold demand: it buys visibility at the exact moment someone has already decided where they want to sleep and is only choosing where to buy. Yet it remains the least used channel among Italian hotels under 100 rooms, often for a simple reason: metasearch gets confused with an OTA.

What metasearch is, and what it is not

A metasearch engine does not sell rooms. It compares: it collects your property's rates from every source publishing them — Booking, Expedia, your own site — and shows them side by side. When the user clicks your direct rate, they leave the metasearch and land on your booking engine.

The difference matters on three levels. The customer is yours: data, email and consent stay with you. The relationship is yours: you can upsell, run pre-stay, build loyalty. And you control the cost: you pay a click or a commission you decide, not a percentage imposed by contract.

What metasearch does not do is generate new demand, and it does not replace Google Ads or social. It does one thing, very well: it converts into a direct booking the demand already heading for your property that today ends up at the OTA by default.

The user's path, step by step

  SEARCH ON GOOGLE
  "hotel [property name]" / "4 star hotel Ischia"
         │
         ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RATE BOX (metasearch)                    │
  │                                            │
  │   Booking.com ............... € 140        │
  │   Expedia ................... € 143        │
  │   Official site ............. € 132   ◀──  │  your direct rate
  │                                            │
  └────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                       │  click on the direct rate
                       ▼
             ┌─────────────────────┐
             │  THE HOTEL'S SITE   │   parity or a better price
             │  booking engine     │   loads in < 2.5 s
             └──────────┬──────────┘
                        ▼
             ┌─────────────────────┐
             │ DIRECT              │   0% commission
             │ BOOKING             │   customer data in house
             └──────────┬──────────┘
                        ▼
              upsell • pre-stay • returning guest

The four platforms: where the volume actually is

Platform Traffic volume in Italy Cost model Average booking value When it is worth it
Google Hotel Ads Very high — 65–75% of metasearch traffic CPC, commission CPA, fixed CPA, Free Booking Links €380 – €620 Always. It is the main channel, at any size
Trivago Medium to high — strong in Germany, Austria, the Netherlands CPC (auction) and CPA €290 – €480 Properties with a strong German-speaking market
TripAdvisor Medium — qualified traffic, but declining CPC and sponsored placements €340 – €560 Anyone with a strong review ranking to defend
Kayak / Trip.com Low in Italy, significant in the US and Asia CPC €400 – €700 Only with a meaningful long-haul mix and a mature budget

The practical reading is clear: if you have one budget, it all goes to Google Hotel Ads. Trivago is the second channel for anyone with a German-speaking share above 25%, TripAdvisor for anyone with strong reviews to defend. Kayak and Trip.com come later.

The three pricing models

The cost model is not a contractual detail: it decides who carries the risk of the campaign, you or the platform.

  • CPC — you pay per click. You pay for every visit that reaches your booking engine, converting or not. The risk is entirely yours, but so is the control: you can push the markets that convert best and reach a very low cost per booking. It does require a booking engine that converts, otherwise you are funding traffic that bounces.
  • Commission CPA — you pay only on a booking. Typically 10–15% of the stay value, charged only when the booking happens. Almost no risk, and still less than an OTA, which takes 15–22% and the customer. It is the right starting point for anyone who has never done metasearch.
  • Fixed CPA. A locked percentage, no auction, visibility managed by the algorithm. Volume is less controllable but the cost is predictable to the cent: suitable for anyone who wants a certain budget line and no daily management.

The rule as you mature: start on commission CPA to build history and learn how well your own site actually converts. After three to six months, if the cost per booking on CPA is consistently above what CPC would give you, move to CPC on your best markets and leave CPA on the rest. A hybrid model is the most common configuration among properties achieving the highest returns.

Google Hotel Ads in detail: the main channel

Google Hotel Ads is the rate box that appears on your hotel's panel in Google Search, Google Maps and the travel section. It concentrates the large majority of metasearch traffic and holds the hottest moment of the whole funnel: the search for your name.

Getting started: you need a connectivity partner

You do not connect to Google directly. You need a connectivity partner — typically your channel manager or booking engine — sending Google rates and availability in real time. Octorate, SiteMinder, D-EDGE and The Hotels Network are among the most common partners for Italian properties; most modern booking engines offer the connection as a module.

The first question to ask your supplier is not "how much does it cost" but "are you already a certified Google connectivity partner?". If the answer is no, the cost of changing supplier belongs in the budget for the metasearch project, because without the connection there is no starting point.

Free Booking Links against paid campaigns

Since 2021 Google has also shown direct booking links free of charge, beneath the paid positions. These are the Free Booking Links: if your booking engine is connected, your official rate appears in the box at no cost. Paid campaigns buy the higher position and a far larger share of impressions, but basic presence is free.

Google Business Profile matters here

The rate box lives inside your Google Business Profile. Up-to-date photographs, correct hours, the right category, recent reviews and replies to them are not an image exercise: they raise the click-through rate on the rate box and therefore lower your cost per booking at the same spend. Before investing in metasearch, fix the profile.

📌 Free Booking Links have been free since 2021. If your booking engine is connected to Google, you appear in the rate box without paying a cent. It is the first step of a metasearch project, at zero cost: switch on the connection, check that the direct rate appears correctly, measure for 30 to 60 days how many bookings arrive free. Only then decide how much budget to put behind paid campaigns — with real data rather than an estimate.

Realistic budget and expected return by size

Property size Suggested monthly budget Starting model Expected bookings per month Expected return once settled
Up to 10 rooms €0 – €150 Free Booking Links only 2 – 6 Not applicable (no cost)
20 – 30 rooms €250 – €500 Commission CPA at 12% 8 – 18 7:1 – 9:1
50 – 60 rooms €600 – €1,200 CPA plus CPC on the top markets 22 – 45 8:1 – 11:1
100+ rooms €1,500 – €4,000 CPC with bids per market 60 – 140 9:1 – 14:1

A return of 8:1 means every euro spent generates eight of gross revenue. Compared with the average 18% OTA commission — equivalent to roughly 5.5:1 on the same booking — the economic advantage is plain, and on top of it the customer stays yours.

Is your hotel already in Google's rate box?

We check free of charge whether your booking engine is connected, whether the direct rate appears, whether you have parity with the OTAs, and how much budget would make sense at your size. Answer within 48 hours, no commitment.

Request the free check Message us on WhatsApp

Five conditions for not burning budget

Metasearch is unforgiving: it amplifies whatever is downstream. If the site converts badly, the campaign simply buys more failures. Five conditions must be met before switching on a paid campaign.

  • Rate parity at least matching the OTA. If your direct price is higher than Booking's in the same box, the user sees the comparison and picks the other. You are paying to demonstrate that you are worse value. Parity is the minimum; a small advantage is better, even just breakfast included and stated in the box.
  • A mobile booking engine under 2.5 seconds. More than 70% of metasearch clicks come from phones. Every second beyond the threshold costs a double-digit share of conversion — on traffic you have already paid for.
  • Availability always current. You need a channel manager syncing in real time. A rate shown in the box and unavailable on the site produces a guaranteed abandonment and, if it repeats, a visibility penalty from the platform.
  • Conversion tracking configured. Tracking on the booking engine, the booking value passed through, attribution verified. Without the monetary value in the platform, the algorithm optimises blind and you do not know what you are buying.
  • Enough budget to leave the learning phase. Below 20 to 30 conversions a month the algorithm has too little data to optimise. One properly funded channel beats four underfunded ones.

Six typical mistakes and what they cost

Mistake What happens Estimated cost over 12 months
Broken rate parity (direct more expensive) Paid clicks that convert on the competing OTA −45% conversion · €4,000 – €9,000 of lost revenue
Slow mobile booking engine (over 4s) Abandonment before the rate is even seen −30% conversion · €3,000 – €7,000
No conversion tracking Blind optimisation, wrong bids for months €2,500 – €6,000 of misallocated budget
A budget too small and too fragmented You never leave the learning phase Money spent for nothing, return under 3:1
The same bid on every market You pay as much for Brazil as for Germany, which converts four times better −25% efficiency · €1,800 – €4,500
Campaigns that do not exclude already-acquired brand traffic You rebuy clicks from people who were coming anyway €1,200 – €3,000 of cannibalisation

The first mistake is worth more on its own than the other five combined, and it is the most common: it almost always comes from promotions published on the OTAs and forgotten on the site.

A real case: a 60-room four-star on Ischia

A seasonal property open April to October, 60 rooms, average ADR €178, 74% of sales through the OTAs. Starting from nothing: no Google connection, booking engine not linked, direct rate absent from the box. The project ran in two phases — Free Booking Links for 60 days first, then Google Hotel Ads on commission CPA at 12%, moving to market-differentiated CPC bids in the second season.

The €5,802 accounting saving is the least interesting part of the result. The real value is the 218 email addresses now in the property's database: customers reachable with pre-stay, upselling and seasonal reactivation at zero acquisition cost in the years ahead — impossible with the same booking arriving from an OTA.

I thought metasearch was advertising, and I had always seen advertising as a gamble. It is accounting instead: I pay 5.7% instead of 18% on exactly the same bookings. What convinced me was the free first phase — 47 bookings in two months without spending anything, just by connecting the booking engine. After that, putting budget behind it was no longer a leap in the dark.

— Manager, 60-room four-star hotel, Ischia

A 45-day activation roadmap

Days 1–10 — Diagnosis. Check rate parity across every channel, test the booking engine's speed on mobile, review the Google Business Profile, confirm your supplier is a certified connectivity partner.

Days 11–20 — Technical foundations. Switch on the rate connection, publish the Free Booking Links, configure conversion tracking with monetary value, and run an end-to-end test of a real booking from the box through to the PMS.

Days 21–35 — Measure at zero cost. Two weeks of free presence only: how many impressions, how many clicks, how many bookings. That is the baseline you size the budget against, and meanwhile you correct any rate or availability mismatches.

Days 36–45 — The paid campaign. Start on commission CPA in your main markets, with a budget sized to your property, a weekly review of the first 30 days, and bids differentiated by market as soon as the data allows.

⚠️ Do not start paid campaigns before fixing rate parity and booking engine speed. With direct more expensive than the OTA, or an engine that takes five seconds, you are buying traffic that does not convert: you pay the click, the user compares, picks Booking, and you have funded the intermediary's commission. Both checks cost an afternoon and are worth more than any later campaign optimisation.

💡 Before raising the budget, always compare the cost per booking against the equivalent OTA commission. While you stay under 10% of the stay value you are gaining on every booking you move across: that threshold tells you when to push and when to stop, far better than the return multiple in the abstract.

In closing

Metasearch is not a creative channel and it is not an advertising gamble: it is a margin operation. The bookings it catches were coming to your property anyway — the only question is at what price. item.title: WhatsApp Business for Hotels and Tour Operators: The Channel That Converts 45%
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Email has an open rate of 21%. WhatsApp has 98%, with an average reply in 90 seconds. And one figure matters more than all the others: if a customer writes to you on WhatsApp and you answer within five minutes, you convert 45% of enquiries. After thirty minutes you are down to 11%. The product has not changed, the price has not changed: only the response time has. For a hotel or tour operator in Campania, this is the single commercial lever with the best cost-to-impact ratio available today.

Why WhatsApp is the number one channel for tourism in Italy

In Italy, WhatsApp penetration on active smartphones is above 97%. It is not an app your customers might have: it is the app they use to talk to their family, their accountant and their mechanic. When they use it to talk to you, they are not learning a new tool, they are just adding a contact.

The advantage is even stronger with international guests. German, Spanish, Brazilian, Dutch and Middle Eastern travellers use WhatsApp as their primary messaging channel: the moment they land at Naples airport the app already works, with no SMS roaming and no need to download your hotel's own application — which, statistically, nobody downloads for a three-night stay.

The third reason is friction. An enquiry through a website form requires the customer to fill in five fields, accept a privacy policy and hope for a reply. An enquiry on WhatsApp is a message written in ten seconds while queuing at a till. The number of enquiries you receive is not a constant: it depends on how easy they are to make.

📌 The figure that changes the perspective: in Italian properties that have made WhatsApp an official channel, total inbound enquiry volume grows on average 60–140% in the first six months. You are not moving enquiries from one channel to another: you are capturing demand that previously did not arrive at all.

WhatsApp against the other channels

Channel Open rate Average response time Enquiry-to-booking conversion Cost per contact
WhatsApp 98% 90 seconds 38–45% (replying within 5 min) €0.00–0.09
Email 21% 6–24 hours 8–12% €0.001–0.01
Telephone n/a (48% of calls missed in high season) Immediate, if someone answers 30–34% €1.80–3.50 (staff cost)
Website live chat 34% engagement among visitors 2–8 minutes 17–21% €0.40–1.20

The phone converts well, but only on the calls you answer: in July and August, with reception under pressure, nearly half go unanswered and nobody calls back. Live chat only works while the visitor is on the site: close the browser and the conversation dies. WhatsApp is the only asynchronous channel with read rates typical of a synchronous one — the conversation stays open even weeks later.

Business App or Business API: the difference that matters

This is where the most common mistake happens. Many properties switch on the free app, use it badly, conclude that "WhatsApp does not work" and go back to email. They are two different products with different uses.

WhatsApp Business App: free, manual, with a clear ceiling

It is the app you download from the store. Free, installed in ten minutes, offering a product catalogue, quick replies, an away message and labels for organising contacts. It runs on one main device with up to four linked devices.

It is perfectly fine for a B&B, a small hotel up to around 30 rooms, or a tour operator with fewer than 15 departures a week. Below 500 messages a month and with a single person answering, the API would be expensive over-engineering. The limit arrives when you need several people answering at once, when you want automatic messages triggered from the PMS, or when you need to track who answered what.

WhatsApp Business API: the channel becomes infrastructure

The API is not an app: it is programmatic access activated through a certified provider — Twilio, 360dialog, Sendbird and Callbell are among the most used in Italy. It gives you multiple operators with queues and assignment, trigger-based automation, two-way integration with your PMS, channel manager and CRM, pre-approved templates for outbound messages, and real reporting.

The cost has two parts: the provider's platform fee (roughly €39–150 a month for an average property) and a per-conversation charge billed by Meta.

Criterion Business App (free) Business API (via a provider)
Property size Up to ~30 rooms / fewer than 15 tours a week Over 30 rooms / more than 15 tours a week / several sites
Messages per month Up to 500 Over 500
People answering at once 1 main device plus 4 linked Unlimited, with queues, assignment and shifts
Automation Quick replies and an away message Conditional flows, AI chatbot, triggers from the PMS
PMS / channel manager / CRM integration None Two-way via API
Meta-approved templates Not available Required for outbound messages
Reporting Basic counts Response times, conversion, revenue attribution
Cost €0 €39–150/month plus per-conversation charges

Meta-approved templates: what they are and what they cost

The fundamental rule: you can write freely to a user only within 24 hours of their last message. Outside that window, any message you start must use a pre-approved template — text submitted to Meta, with dynamic variables in braces, which is reviewed and approved, usually within hours, sometimes in a day or two.

This is not bureaucracy for its own sake: it is the mechanism that has kept WhatsApp free of spam, and why open rates remain at 98%. There are three categories, priced differently.

Template category What it is for A tourism example Indicative cost per conversation (Italy)
Utility Updates on a transaction in progress Booking confirmation, check-in reminder, pre-check-in link €0.03–0.04
Marketing Promotions, offers, reactivation Transfer upsell, last-minute offer, seasonal reactivation €0.08–0.10
Authentication Verification and access codes One-time codes for a guest area or self check-in €0.04–0.06
Service (started by the user) Replies within the 24-hour window All in-stay assistance €0.00

The fact that service conversations are free changes the economics of guest care: answering a guest who writes to you has no marginal cost. You pay only when you start the conversation, and you pay more when you do so to sell.

How a conversation moves, from message to operator

  INCOMING MESSAGE
         │
         ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  CONTACT             │  number already in the CRM?
  │  RECOGNITION         │  active booking in the PMS?
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │
      ┌──────┴───────┐
      │              │
   KNOWN           NEW
      │              │
      ▼              ▼
 ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
 │ Live    │   │ Welcome +    │
 │ stay    │   │ opt-in +     │
 │ context │   │ quick menu   │
 └────┬────┘   └──────┬───────┘
      └───────┬───────┘
              ▼
   ┌────────────────────────┐
   │  AUTOMATION / AI BOT   │
   │  hours, wifi,          │
   │  availability, rates   │
   └───────────┬────────────┘
               │
          resolved?
       ┌───────┴────────┐
      YES               NO
       │                 │
       ▼                 ▼
 ┌──────────┐   ┌─────────────────┐
 │ Close    │   │ HANDOVER TO A   │
 │ + log to │   │ PERSON          │
 │ CRM      │   │ queue, SLA <5min│
 └──────────┘   └────────┬────────┘
                         ▼
                ┌─────────────────┐
                │ QUOTE /         │
                │ PAYMENT LINK    │
                │ → PMS/booking   │
                └─────────────────┘

The critical point in that diagram is the handover: a bot that does not know when to pass over destroys more value than it creates. The working rule is simple: two failed automatic attempts, or any keyword touching price, availability or a complaint, and the conversation goes to a person.

The six automations that generate the most value

You do not need to automate everything. In accommodation, six flows cover more than 80% of the available value.

1. Booking confirmation and arrival instructions

Triggered automatically when the booking enters the PMS. It contains the summary, the location with a map link, check-in times and parking directions — which in Naples and on the Amalfi Coast is the number one question. It cuts "how do I get to you?" phone calls and reduces no-shows on direct bookings.

2. Pre-check-in with document collection

Sent 48 hours before arrival with a link to the registration form and document upload. The guest fills it in from their sofa, not standing at the desk with a suitcase in hand. It is the automation that frees the most minutes at reception.

3. Pre-stay upselling

Sent five to seven days before arrival. Airport transfers, room upgrades, dinner at the property, an excursion to Pompeii or by boat. The timing is ideal: the guest has already decided to come, is planning their days and is at the most receptive point of the cycle.

4. Assistance during the stay

Wifi password, breakfast times, extra towels, restaurant bookings, taxis. Service conversations, therefore free, replacing the internal phone and reducing trips to the desk.

5. Review request after check-out

Sent three or four hours after departure, while the memory is fresh and the guest is travelling with their phone in hand. The response rate on WhatsApp is three to five times that of the same request by email.

6. Seasonal reactivation of returning guests

Sent 10 or 11 months after the previous stay, before the guest starts searching Booking again. It is the highest-margin conversation you can have: no commission, no acquisition cost, just a nine-cent marketing template.

Want to know which of these six to switch on first?

We analyse your enquiry volume, the PMS you use and your current response times, and tell you where the fastest return is. No commitment.

Request the free analysis Message us on WhatsApp

Automation Trigger Template type Expected response Value generated
Confirmation and arrival instructions Booking confirmed in the PMS Utility 96% read / 31% reply −40% pre-arrival calls, fewer no-shows
Pre-check-in with documents 48h before arrival Utility 68–74% completion −4 minutes per check-in at the desk
Pre-stay upselling 7 days before arrival Marketing 18–24% conversion €18–42 extra per room
In-stay assistance The guest's message Service (free) 100% Higher NPS, lighter load on reception
Review request 3h after check-out Utility 27–33% 3–5× the reviews email produces
Returning guest reactivation 10–11 months after the stay Marketing 9–14% book Direct bookings at zero commission

⚠️ GDPR and Meta's policies: do not improvise here. You need explicit, documented opt-in before writing to a contact first — a checkbox at booking, a form on the site, a QR code at the property, as long as the date and source are recorded. Consent for marketing messages is separate from consent for transactional ones: a guest may want their booking confirmation and not your offers. Remember the 24-hour window: outside it you can only write using approved templates. And never buy lists of numbers: besides being unlawful, a high block rate lowers your number's quality rating until the account is suspended, and recovering it takes a long time.

WhatsApp is not a silo: fitting it into the rest of the stack

The structural mistake is treating WhatsApp as a separate inbox, on a company phone where only one person knows what has been said. If the conversation does not reach the CRM, the value evaporates as soon as that person goes on holiday.

The sensible minimum integration has three points. The PMS is the source of triggers: booking created, changed, imminent, closed. The channel manager supplies real availability, so when a customer asks "do you have a double from the 12th to the 15th?" the answer is verified rather than "I'll let you know". The CRM holds the history: every conversation enriches the guest profile, so at the next enquiry the operator already knows this is a returning guest who took the transfer last year.

On top of those three, an AI chatbot handles the first level around the clock — the repetitive questions, the night-time ones, the ones in languages nobody on the team speaks. The bot does not replace the operator: it filters the noise and leaves them the conversations that matter.

💡 If you can only switch on one, switch on pre-check-in. It is the highest-return automation for a hotel: it cuts reception time at the worst moment of the day, reduces document transcription errors and — a detail almost nobody uses — opens the upsell conversation naturally. A guest who has just uploaded their documents on WhatsApp is one message away from "shall we book your airport transfer?".

A real case: a Naples tour operator, 8 staff, 40 tours a week

An inbound operator based in Naples, eight people, averaging 40 departures a week across Pompeii, Vesuvius, the Amalfi Coast and boat tours. Starting point: enquiries arriving on five different channels — email, website form, Messenger, telephone and the owner's personal WhatsApp — with no tracking and no shifts. In high season the average first response took more than five hours, and nobody knew how many enquiries were being lost.

What changed: migration to the WhatsApp Business API with a dedicated number, integration with the booking system, six automations running and a first-level AI bot in four languages.

KPI Before After 12 months Change
Enquiries handled per month 310 724 +134%
Average first response time 5h 20min 2 min (bot) / 9 min (person) −97%
Enquiry-to-booking conversion 16% 37% +21 points
Extra bookings per month — 94 +94
Average booking value €161 €168 +4%
Team hours a week on messaging 31 9 −22 hours
Attributed extra annual revenue — €189,500 —
Platform plus conversation cost — €4,920/year 38× return

The 22 hours a week freed up are not an accounting saving: they went into B2B selling to agencies and partner hotels, which added a second revenue stream not counted in the €189,500.

For years I answered customers from my personal number, even at eleven at night, convinced the service was what made the difference. The problem is that when I was out on a tour nobody answered, and those enquiries vanished without a trace. Today the first message goes out in two minutes even at night, and for the first time I know exactly how many enquiries I get and how many I close. What I did not expect is that people write more: ten used to call, now thirty message me.

— Owner, inbound tour operator, Naples

Setting it up in 30 days

Week 1 — Foundations. Verify the business on Meta Business Manager (VAT number, website, verified domain). Choose a dedicated number, never the owner's personal one: the number is a company asset and should be registered to the company. Select the API provider based on the integrations available with your PMS.

Week 2 — Templates and content. Write the six to ten templates in the languages you genuinely need — Italian, English and the two most common among your guests — submit them to Meta for approval, and prepare the business profile: logo, description, hours, address, catalogue.

Week 3 — Automation and integration. Connect the PMS and the channel manager, configure the triggers, define the handover rules to the human team, and run end-to-end tests on real trial bookings.

Week 4 — Team and go live. Train the operators on tone of voice, response times and using the shared queue. Define internal service levels — first response within five minutes during staffed hours. Go live gradually: first with guests who have already booked, then publicly on the site, email signature, Google Business Profile and materials at the property.

📌 One detail worth the whole project: put the wa.me link everywhere the customer meets you — site header and footer, contact page, email signature, Google Business Profile, QR codes in the room and at reception, cards on the tour desks. The channel works in proportion to how easy it is to find.

Related reading

  • AI chatbots for hotels and B&Bs: the digital front desk that works 24/7 — how to build the automatic first level that feeds your WhatsApp conversations.
  • From 5 to 20 bookings a month: one tour agency's path — the complete commercial growth case on digital channels.
  • Email marketing for hotels: pre-stay and post-stay sequences — how to make email and messaging work together without overlapping.

In closing

WhatsApp is not "another channel to cover". It is where demand appears first, in the format your customers already use to talk. The difference between those who use it well and those who merely endure it is not technology — the API is within reach of any property above 30 rooms — but organisation: a company number, well-written templates, automation on the six flows that matter, and a clear rule about when a human takes over.

The opening figure remains the best summary available: 45% conversion within five minutes, 11% after thirty. Everything else is execution.

item.title: Instagram and TikTok for Hotels: The Content Strategy (and the Guest Content) That Fills Rooms
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-one per cent of travellers under 35 choose their destination by watching a video on social, before they ever open Booking. If your property does not appear at that stage, you are not losing a booking: you never enter the shortlist. By the time the guest reaches the OTA they have already decided where to go and often which place to sleep in. You are competing on price in a race that was settled two weeks earlier.

The shift: social is no longer a shop window

For years the logic was: the website sells, social displays. Today it is the other way round. Instagram and TikTok are visual search engines: people type "things to do on the Amalfi Coast" or "hotel with a pool in Sorrento" inside the app, not into Google. And the platform returns videos, not blue links.

Every piece of content therefore needs a search intent inside it: on-screen text, caption and spoken words are all indexed. A Reel titled "Three places ten minutes from the hotel where there is never a queue" is not a nice piece of content, it is an answer to a query that keeps circulating for months.

The second consequence is economic: here reach is bought with time instead of budget. TikTok shows content to people who do not follow you, which no other owned channel does: it is the one place where a fourteen-room property reaches 200,000 people without advertising.

Dimension Instagram TikTok
Dominant demographic 28–50, couples and families, good spend 18–35, experience-led travel, late booking
Dominant format Reels, carousels, Stories Vertical, 15–45 seconds, fast-paced
Organic reach to non-followers Medium (10–25% of impressions) High (60–85% of impressions)
Intent captured Consideration: "does this place convince me?" Discovery: "I didn't know this existed"
When to invest Always: the base for 3–5 star and boutique hotels If you have something visually strong — a view, a pool

📌 The working rule: produce once, publish twice. The same vertical goes to TikTok for discovery and to Instagram Reels for consideration, with different captions. Anyone producing separate content for the two platforms gives up within six weeks.

The minimum sustainable plan: the 40/30/20/10 rule

Hotel profiles do not die from a shortage of ideas, but from the lack of a repeatable format. Four posts a week is the right target: below that you build no rhythm, above it you cannot keep going without a dedicated person. With two hours of filming and editing, four pieces are achievable.

  • 40% place and region. Not your room: Vesuvius at dawn, lemons picked by hand, the beach at seven in the morning. This is the content that travels: nobody saves a photograph of a hotel room, they save a place they want to be.
  • 30% the guest experience. Breakfast on the terrace, the detail of the Vietri ceramics, the sound of the coffee machine. Proof that what you promise actually exists.
  • 20% behind the scenes and people. Staff setting up the dining room, the mozzarella supplier five kilometres away, the cook kneading dough. It has the highest comment rate and it is the only thing nobody can copy from you.
  • 10% a direct offer. One commercial post in every ten: a rate, a package, a last-minute deal. It works because it is rare.

The 90/10 split between value and selling is not ethics, it is mechanics: the platforms distribute according to watch time, and nothing shortens it like a post that sells.

Ten formats that work for an accommodation business

Format Production effort Expected reach Objective
Vertical room tour in one continuous take Low (15 min) Medium Consideration
Time-lapse of sunrise from the terrace Low (setup plus waiting) High Awareness
"Three places ten minutes from here" (local guide) Medium (half a day) Very high Awareness
Breakfast shot first-person, close-ups and sound Low (20 min) High Consideration
Behind the scenes with staff at the start of the day Low (20 min) Medium Consideration
Q&A: answering a question received in a DM Very low (5 min) Medium Consideration
Reposting guest content with written permission None Medium Consideration
The local supplier (dairy, lemon grove) Medium (2 hours) High Awareness
Before and after a refurbishment Low (from the archive) High Awareness
A direct offer with availability and a deadline Very low (10 min) Low Conversion

The funnel: from video to direct booking

Properties do not lose on the content, they lose on the step afterwards: a video with 300,000 views and a link in bio pointing at the home page produces no bookings. The path is a chain, and every link is measurable.

  DISCOVERY              PROFILE           LINK IN BIO        BOOKING ENGINE
  (feed / for you)  (bio + highlights)  (dedicated landing)  (dates + rate)
       │                   │                   │                   │
  ┌────┴─────┐       ┌─────┴──────┐      ┌─────┴──────┐      ┌─────┴──────┐

The numbers are realistic for a small property with one piece of content that did well: 100,000 views produce around 18 direct bookings. At an ADR of €210 over three nights, that video is worth nearly €11,000 of full revenue, with no commission.

Guest content: the material you do not have to produce

Every week your guests shoot dozens of videos at your property, with an advantage your own content will never have: they are credible, because you did not make them. In 95% of cases they disappear within 24 hours into somebody's Stories, never touching your profile.

How to encourage it

Guest content does not happen by accident, it is designed. Four things are needed: a deliberately photogenic corner — a terrace, a staircase with bougainvillea, a breakfast plated to be photographed before it is eaten; a short property hashtag, written in the room, on the menu and in your email signature; a real incentive, an aperitif or a late check-out for anyone who tags you; and a QR code in the room, because when a guest wants to tag you they do not want to go searching.

How to get usage rights

This is where the most expensive mistake lives. Resharing gives you no usage rights. Resharing a Story you are tagged in is tolerated by the platform, but it does not authorise you to use that content on your website, in a paid campaign or on Booking. You need written permission: three lines in a DM — who you are, which content, where and for how long you will use it — with an explicit reply ("yes, I agree") and a screenshot kept. For advertising, a release by email is better.

How to reuse it

Authorised content has four lives: the gallery on your website; Meta campaigns, where it costs 30–50% less per click than a professional photograph; your Booking or Google Business listing; and pre-stay emails, where it raises the take-up of extras. No production, an hour a month to manage.

Does your profile bring bookings, or just likes?

We analyse your Instagram and TikTok free of charge: content mix, the funnel from the link in bio, conversion tracking and unused guest content. A concrete report within 48 hours, no commitment.

Request the free analysis Message us on WhatsApp

Working with creators: how to choose properly

Collaborations are the most effective shortcut to discovery and the fastest way to burn three thousand euros. The difference lies in the selection criteria, which are almost always wrong because they look at follower counts.

The data that matters is different. Engagement rate: below 2% the profile is inflated or exhausted; between 4% and 8% the audience is active. And above all the geographic audience: a creator with 80,000 followers who are 70% Brazilian is useless to an Amalfi Coast hotel selling into the Italian, German and British markets. Always ask for the country and age insights: anyone working seriously sends them straight away.

Third criterion, size. Micro-creators between 5,000 and 30,000 followers convert better than the large accounts: they have a real relationship with their audience and their recommendation carries the weight of a friend's. For the budget of one macro creator you engage four and spread the risk.

Payment model Strengths Weaknesses Cost range (Italy)
Barter / hosting Low marginal cost, fills the low season Little control over timing and quality, many requests 2–3 nights (real cost €80 – €200)
Fixed fee plus hosting Deliverables and usage rights in a contract A certain outlay even if the content underperforms €300 – €1,500 per micro-creator
Fee plus commission on bookings Aligns interests, measurable with a tracked link Needs reliable tracking; few accept it €150 – €600 plus 6–10% of the stay
Macro-creator (100k+) Immediate reach, visibility effect Low engagement, scattered audience €2,000 – €8,000 per campaign

Three things in writing avoid 100% of the problems: the number and type of deliverables (one Reel, three Stories, five raw photographs), the publication window, and usage rights for 12 months, advertising included. Without that last point you pay for content you can only look at.

⚠️ Collaborations must be disclosed. Always. In Italy the competition authority requires transparency in commercial communication: any content arising from an agreement must carry #adv or an equivalent disclosure clearly, at the start of the caption and not buried among twenty hashtags. No exceptions: this applies to pure barter too, where the only payment is the stay. Responsibility is shared and penalties reach the business as well: put it in the agreement as a clause and check the post the same day.

What to measure, and what to ignore

The most-quoted metric is the one that matters least: likes measure a gesture that costs nothing. Saves and shares measure intention — someone who saves a hotel video is planning a trip, someone who shares it is persuading another person to come — and they are the signals the platforms weight most heavily: optimising for saves is optimising for reach.

Then you move down the funnel. Clicks on the link in bio are the first monetisable number. Bookings attributed through UTM parameters are the truth: without tracking on the landing page, everything else is opinion. Finally, the figure that ends the discussion with the owners: cost per social booking against cost per OTA booking. If a social booking costs €38 and the same one from Booking costs 18% of €630 — €113 — the conversation is over.

KPI How it is measured Benchmark for accommodation
Save rate (Reels) Saves / views Good above 1.5% — excellent above 3%
Engagement rate (Likes + comments + saves) / reach 4% – 8%
Reach to non-followers Native per-post insight Instagram above 30% — TikTok above 60%
Clicks on the link in bio Tracked link or UTM 1% – 3% of profile visits
Landing-to-booking conversion Booking engine with source UTM 2% – 5%
Cost per social booking (Hours × hourly cost + fees) / bookings €25 – €60 (against €90 – €140 via OTA)
DM response time Native insight Under 2 hours during the day

A real case: a 14-room boutique hotel on the Amalfi Coast

An independent property, average ADR €240, open April to October, 81% of sales through the OTAs. Instagram stuck on occasional posts of an empty room, no TikTok at all. A twelve-month programme: 40/30/20/10 at four pieces a week, opening TikTok, four micro-creators (two on barter, two on a fee), systematic guest content with a QR code in the room, and a landing page with UTM tracking.

KPI (12 months) Before After
Instagram followers 1,840 11,400
Average monthly reach (Instagram + TikTok) 4,200 186,000
Clicks to the site from social 310 a year 5,900 a year
Direct bookings attributed (UTM) 4 73
Value generated (ADR €240 × 3.1 nights) €2,976 €54,312
Total invested (creators plus production) — €8,900
Return — 6.1× — €122 per booking, €0 OTA commission

The detail that explains the result: 44 of the 73 bookings came from just six pieces of content, all of them "place and region" or made by creators. The other 200 posts built the credibility that let them convert.

For years we published photographs of the rooms, thinking that was what people wanted to see. The video that changed our season is a walk through the village at dawn, filmed on a phone by one of our housekeepers: 400,000 views and twenty-two enquiries in a week. We no longer ask "how do we show the hotel", we ask "why would anyone save this video".

— Manager, 14-room boutique hotel, Amalfi Coast

💡 One Reel that performs is worth more than fifty mediocre posts. If you have two hours a week, do not spread them across five fillers: put them into one strong piece — scout the location, wait for the right light, frame it deliberately, edit it properly. Distribution here has an extreme long tail: almost all the value comes from the few pieces that break through, and five mediocre posts never add up to one good Reel.

The 90-day plan

Days 1–30 — Foundations. Rewrite the bio with location, category and a clear benefit. Create the highlights: rooms, the area, breakfast, how to get here, reviews. Build the landing page connected to the booking engine, with UTMs on every link. Define the property hashtag, print the QR code for the rooms, identify the three photogenic corners. Then start: four pieces a week, TikTok open.

Days 31–60 — Volume and guest content. Keep the rhythm and read the data: which two formats generate the most saves. Set up the guest content process — written permission, an archive, reuse on the site and in emails. Approach eight to ten suitable micro-creators and close the first two collaborations in low season, with a written agreement and a disclosure clause.

Days 61–90 — Amplification and measurement. Move the budget to the two winning formats and put advertising behind the organic content that already performs: it costs less per click because it is validated. Close the other two collaborations for high season and set up monthly reporting on the seven KPIs.

Related reading

  • Increasing direct bookings — social generates demand, but you need a system to convert it without the OTAs.
  • Managing online reviews on Booking and TripAdvisor — the social proof that closes what the video opened.
  • Email marketing for hotels: pre-stay and post-stay — where to reuse guest content and how to turn a follower into a guest.

In closing

Instagram and TikTok are not a channel to hand to an intern: they are where the destination is decided, before there is any Booking search to win. Whoever enters that stage builds their own demand; whoever is absent buys someone else's, at 18% commission, for ever.

The work required is less than it looks — four pieces a week, an hour a month on guest content, a few well-chosen collaborations — but it has to be done with the discipline of a system, not the enthusiasm of a month. The €54,000 on the Amalfi Coast came from twelve months of steady rhythm, a tracked funnel, and six pieces that broke through because two hundred others had laid the ground.

item.title: Getting Found by ChatGPT: How to Enter the Answers of AI Assistants (Hotels and Tour Operators)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
One of your potential guests has just asked ChatGPT "where should I stay in Sorrento with the children, near the sea, under €150". They got four names back. They did not open Google, did not look at Booking, did not see an advertisement. They read four names and picked one. If yours was not among them, as far as that customer is concerned you do not exist — and you did not notice, because no lost visit shows up in your statistics.

It is the quietest change in tourism of the past two years. There is no drop in traffic to raise the alarm: it is simply that part of the decision is now taken somewhere else, before anyone reaches your website. This guide explains how it actually works, what can be measured and what can be done — without promising shortcuts that do not exist.

What changed: from "searching" to "asking"

For twenty years the route was always the same: the user typed something, Google showed ten links, the user clicked. All the SEO we know exists to get into those ten links.

With a conversational assistant the shape of that route changes. The user describes a situation — not a keyword — and receives one answer, not a list. Inside that answer there are two or three names, five at most. There is no second page.

The difference that matters: in Google's results, being tenth means receiving few clicks. In a conversational answer, being "eleventh" means not being named at all. There is no long tail: either you are in the answer, or you are not there.

Where an assistant gets its information

Simplifying, from three places:

  1. What it learned during training. General information, often not very recent, about well-known places and properties.
  2. What it reads at the time of asking. Almost every assistant, when the question calls for current data, goes and reads web pages in real time. This is where the game is played.
  3. What it finds in aggregated sources. Portals, directories, reviews, third-party listings.

Point two is the only one you can act on directly, and it is also the one that weighs most on the concrete questions — prices, availability, amenities, location.

It is not an entirely new phenomenon: it is the same direction taken by voice search, where the user already asks a question and receives a single answer. Conversational assistants have carried that model out of the kitchen and into the moment of the buying decision.

They are not all the same

"Getting found by AI" is a simplification: the assistants behave differently, and it helps to know which one you are trying to reach.

  • ChatGPT generates the most volume, and when the question concerns availability or prices it goes and reads the web then and there. It is also the one that, in the logs of the sites we look after, passes by most often.
  • Perplexity cites its sources explicitly, with the links on show: it is the assistant most likely to send you an actual visit, because the link is clickable.
  • Google AI Overviews is the summary that appears above the search results. It is not a separate assistant: it draws on the same pages Google has already indexed. Here the SEO you have already done continues to count.
  • Gemini and Copilot follow logic close to Google's and Bing's: indexing and structured data are what matter.

The good news is that the work to be done is largely the same for all of them. The bad news is that there is no lever for "optimising for ChatGPT" separate from everything else.

How much is really happening: the numbers from a real site

On one of the sites we look after — a tour agency in Campania — we measured the reads made by AI assistant crawlers. Over roughly two months: just under 65,000 reads, 78% of them from ChatGPT, spread across some thirty different agents. Before that period, the same measurement returned zero.

Be careful how you read that figure. Those 65,000 are not visits by people: they are automated reads. They measure how much the assistants are consulting the site, not how many customers it brings. It is a distinction many suppliers blur, sometimes deliberately, because the number is large and makes an impression.

The figure that concerns people, on the same site, is a different one: 0.7% of real visits arrive from an AI assistant. That is not much. But two years ago it was zero, and the curve is rising.

This is the honest picture: today the assistants read a great deal and send very little. Anyone who gets organised now does so while the cost is low and the competition is looking elsewhere.

Are the AI assistants reading your site? We will check

We analyse your server logs and tell you which crawlers come by, which pages they read, what is blocking them and what is missing for you to be cited. A concrete report within 48 hours, no commitment.

Request the free analysis Message us on WhatsApp

What makes a site readable by an assistant

There is no trick. There are conditions that make a page usable by a machine which has to summarise it in two lines.

1. Answer the question instead of circling it

An assistant looks for sentences that answer on their own. "Check-in is from 2pm to 8pm; after 8pm on request, with a €20 supplement" is quotable. "Our staff will be delighted to welcome you at whatever time suits you best" is not: it contains no information.

The same holds for everything: prices, distances, cancellation policies, pets, parking, opening hours. Every piece of information a customer would ask for on the telephone should exist on the site as a clear, self-contained sentence.

2. Structured data, done properly

Structured data (schema.org) is the standard way of telling a machine "this is a hotel, this is the price, this is the location, this is the star rating". For an accommodation business you need at least:

  • Hotel or LodgingBusiness with address, coordinates, telephone and price range
  • FAQPage covering the questions you actually receive
  • Product or Offer for rooms and packages, if you sell direct
  • Review and AggregateRating, if you have reviews of your own
To do today, free: open the schema.org validator and paste in your home page address. If nothing comes out, or errors do, you have found the first job on the list.

3. Do not block the crawlers without knowing it

Many sites block the assistants' bots in their robots.txt file, sometimes because somebody copied a configuration found online, sometimes because a security plugin does it automatically. The user agents worth checking today are at least GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended.

Blocking them is a legitimate choice — but it has to be a choice, not an accident. If you block them, you accept not appearing in the answers.

4. Content somebody would quote

Assistants favour sources that answer specific questions precisely. For a property in Campania, pages like "How to get to Sorrento from Naples airport" or "Where to park in Positano" are worth more than an "About us" page: they are exactly what somebody asks an assistant, and you can answer better than a general portal because you live there.

It is the same material local SEO needs, and the same that feeds an assistant on your own site: written once, it works on three fronts.

5. Be consistent everywhere

If your site says check-in is at 2pm, your Google Business Profile says 3pm and Booking says 4pm, an assistant has no way of knowing whom to believe — and it tends not to cite a source that contradicts itself. Address, telephone, opening hours and amenities have to match across every listing.

6. Have reviews, and have them visible

When an assistant has to choose between two equivalent properties, it looks at public judgement: average score, number of reviews, what they say. It is not a factor you can touch by writing code — it is built up over time by managing your reviews. But it is worth knowing that it counts here too, not only on Booking.

How to check whether they name you

There is no mature tool yet, nothing like Search Console. In the meantime, two methods that work:

The manual test. Put the questions one of your customers would ask to three or four different assistants. Not "hotels in Sorrento", but "I'm going to Sorrento in June with two small children, looking for somewhere near the sea without spending too much". Write down who gets named. Repeat every month: it is a crude measure, but it is a measure.

The server logs. Crawler reads leave a trace. Filtering the user agents shows which assistants come by, how often and which pages they read. It is the most solid data available today, and it is where the figures quoted above come from.

An early indicator: if the crawlers read a lot but visits from assistants stay at zero, the problem is usually in the content — they read you and find nothing worth quoting. If they do not read you at all, the problem is technical: robots.txt, firewall blocks, pages that only build themselves with JavaScript.

What does not work

A certain amount of nonsense is already circulating. For the avoidance of doubt:

  • You cannot buy a position inside ChatGPT's answers the way you buy an advertisement on Google. Anyone offering you that is selling something else.
  • Stuffing your pages with "AI", "artificial intelligence" and the like does nothing. It is the 2026 edition of keyword stuffing, and it works about as well.
  • Mass-generated text published without review makes things worse. Assistants are trained to recognise generic content; a page that adds nothing does not get cited, and meanwhile it dilutes your site.
  • It is not a substitute for SEO. Google remains by far the first channel. This is one more channel, to be cultivated while the other keeps working.

Where to start, in order

If you have to choose what to do first:

  1. Check your robots.txt. Ten minutes. If you are blocking the assistants' crawlers without meaning to, nothing else you do will have any effect.
  2. Put structured data on the home page and on the room or tour pages. That is the foundation.
  3. Rewrite the "service" pages so that they contain real answers: hours, prices, distances, rules. No courtesy phrases standing in for information.
  4. Align the external listings — Google Business Profile, Booking, TripAdvisor — with what the site says.
  5. Write three pages answering concrete local questions you get on the telephone.
  6. Measure, and measure again in three months.

The questions we are asked most

Should I block the AI crawlers to protect my content?

It depends what you sell. If you live on original content — guides, itineraries, photography — blocking them is a defensible position. If you sell rooms or tours, the content on your site exists to get you chosen: blocking whoever reads it means giving up on appearing. For an accommodation business, in the great majority of cases it is better to let them in.

How long before I see an effect?

Crawlers come back in days or weeks, depending on how often the site is updated. Being cited in the answers is slower, because it also depends on external sources and on the competition for that particular question. Reasonably: a few weeks to be re-read, a few months to measure a difference.

Do I need a plugin or a paid tool?

No. Structured data, a correct robots.txt and well-written pages are done with what you already have. There are AI citation monitoring tools, useful if you manage many sites; for a single property, the monthly manual test and the server logs are enough.

I'm on Booking — don't they find me already?

They find you, but as a line in somebody else's list. Assistants readily cite the big portals, and in that answer the name that sticks is the portal's: the booking goes through them, with the commission that follows. Appearing in your own right is exactly the work that increases direct bookings.

Does AI-written content help you get found by AI?

No, and it usually does damage. An assistant is looking for information it cannot find elsewhere: opening hours, prices, real distances, the advice of somebody who lives in the place. Generic text generated in bulk contains none of that, and meanwhile it lowers the average quality of your site.

In short

AI assistants are already reading your site — or skipping it. Today they bring a small share of visits, and anyone telling you otherwise is overstating it. But it is a share that did not exist two years ago, and the conditions for being cited are built now, with work that is worth doing anyway: clear information, tidy data, consistency across channels.

It is the same work that makes a site useful to a person. The difference is that somebody else is now reading it first.

We start from your site, not from a theory

We check robots.txt, structured data, consistency across your external listings and the crawler reads. Then we tell you, in order, the three things to fix first.

item.title: The CIN and the EU Short-Term Rental Regulation: What Is Actually Being Checked from 2026
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
You have the CIN. It is in the drawer, with the printout of the receipt from the national database. But then on Booking the listing is in the company's name, on Airbnb it is in yours, the street number is written two different ways, and on one of the two portals the code was never entered at all because "they asked for it in a field nobody could make sense of". As long as nobody was checking, it was harmless untidiness. From 2026 it is not, because what does the checking is not an inspector ringing the doorbell: it is an automated comparison between two databases.

This guide explains how the two overlapping layers of rules work today — Italy's CIN and the European short-term rental Regulation — what actually changes for anyone letting a property, and where things most often break. It contains no penalty amounts: at the end we explain why, and where to find them kept up to date.

The picture in two lines

There are two overlapping sets of rules, and they are often confused.

  • The CIN is Italian. The Codice Identificativo Nazionale — national identification code — comes from article 13-ter of decree-law 145/2023 (as converted by law 191/2023): a code assigned by the Ministry of Tourism to every unit used for short-term or tourist letting and to every accommodation business. It has to be requested, displayed and published in your listings.
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1028 is European and applies from 20 May 2026. It does not create a new code: it sets common rules on how member states' registration systems must work and on what data the platforms must transmit to the authorities.
The distinction that matters: the European Regulation imposes no new obligation on you directly. It does not require states to set up a register: it says that if they do, it must follow harmonised rules. Italy already has its register. So the practical effect is not "one more obligation": it is that the obligation you already have becomes verifiable automatically.

The CIN: who needs one and where it goes

It applies to anyone carrying on a hospitality activity: short-term lets, holiday homes, rooms to let, B&Bs, farm stays, hotels. You apply for it through the Ministry of Tourism's BDSR portal — the Banca Dati delle Strutture Ricettive, the national accommodation database — using the digital identity (SPID or electronic ID card) of the owner or legal representative.

The step that blocks the most applications comes earlier: in many regions the CIN will not be generated unless the property already has its regional code. If the national database cannot find the property, the portal is not malfunctioning — the regional registration is missing. That is where you start.

The three places the code has to appear

  1. In every online listing, on any channel: OTA portals, your own website, classified listings, social media if you use it to sell.
  2. Outside the property, where the rules require it.
  3. In the national database, with the unit's details correct and up to date — and this is the reference everything else gets compared against.

If you run several channels, entering the code by hand on each one is the quickest way to forget one. Anyone working through a channel manager sets it once on the property record and it propagates to every connected listing: this is exactly the kind of repetitive compliance task that tool exists for.

What changed on 20 May 2026

From spring 2026 the European Regulation is fully applicable. Three mechanisms, in summary.

1. The platforms verify the code, they no longer just collect it

Previously the registration number was a text field: you typed something and the listing went live. Now the platforms have to check that the code exists and is valid by comparing it against the public registers, identify irregular listings and remove them at the authorities' request.

In plain terms: a wrong, expired or mismatched code is no longer inert data in a form. It is a discrepancy that surfaces by itself.

2. Activity data reaches the authorities periodically

The platforms transmit information about the lettings to the public authorities: the number of nights booked, data relating to guests, the address and the identifier of the accommodation. Not on a case-by-case request — periodically and in a structured form.

3. A single digital entry point

The flow does not go through bilateral arrangements between each portal and each municipality: it goes through one national single digital entry point. It is the least visible part and the most consequential, because it is what makes comparison possible at scale rather than on a sample basis.

What the Regulation does NOT do. It introduces no ban on letting, sets no maximum number of nights, does not harmonise taxes and does not replace Italian, regional or municipal rules: it is added to them. Local tourist tax, the obligation to report guests to the police, municipal caps and regional requirements all continue to apply exactly as before. Anyone telling you that "Europe has liberalised it" or "Europe has banned it" is oversimplifying in both directions.

The practical consequence: consistency is no longer a detail

This is the part worth the read. Until yesterday your information lived in separate compartments: the national database, the listings on the portals, the police guest-reporting portal, the tourist tax return, the accounts. Nobody compared them, except in a specific investigation.

Now the pipes connecting them exist. Which means a difference between two systems does not stay hidden: it stands out as an anomaly without anyone having gone looking for it.

There are four alignments to check:

  • Code → unit. The CIN published in a listing has to correspond to the unit that listing actually sells. With two apartments in the same building, swapping them is a three-second copy-and-paste mistake.
  • Address → national database. Street, number, flat and postcode written the way the database recorded them, not the way you usually write them.
  • Nights sold → nights declared. The nights the portal reports and the nights appearing in your tourist tax return should be the same number.
  • Guests → police reporting. Reporting your guests to the provincial police headquarters remains a separate obligation, with its own deadlines. The European data flow does not replace it.

We will check whether your listings line up

Channel by channel, we verify that the CIN is present and correct, that the address and unit details match the national database, and that no old listings are still live in your name. A precise report, no commitment.

Request the check Message us on WhatsApp

Where things break, in order of frequency

From what we see on clients' sites and accounts, the mistakes are almost always the same five — and not one of them is a mistake in reading the law. They are management problems.

1. The code is on two channels out of four. Entered on Booking and Airbnb the day it was issued, never added to the property's own website or to the secondary portal opened the year before. The own website is the one most often forgotten, because "it's ours".

2. An old listing is still live. A page on a minor portal, opened by a former colleague and never closed, with no code and a price from three seasons ago. It is still yours in the eyes of whoever is comparing the data.

3. The address is written three different ways. "Via Roma 12", "Via Roma, 12/A", "V. Roma 12 int. 3". To a person they are the same place. To an automated comparison they are three addresses.

4. The registered holder is not the one taking the money. Property registered in an individual's name, listings in the company's name (or the other way round). It is the most tedious discrepancy to fix, because it means touching the registration rather than the listing.

5. The regional code is missing and nobody knows. The CIN application failed months earlier, the error message was taken for a portal glitch, and work has continued without a code in the belief that one was requested.

What to check today, in half an hour

  1. List every active channel. All of them: OTAs, your own site, local portals, pages on consortium websites, classifieds. Search the property's name on Google to find the ones you have forgotten.
  2. Verify the code on each, character by character, against the database receipt and not against memory.
  3. Compare the address on every listing with the one registered in the national database, in the same form.
  4. Close the listings you no longer use. Not "pause" them: close them.
  5. Check the ownership: whoever is the registered holder in the database and whoever appears as host on the portals have to be the same person or entity.
  6. Reconcile one sample month: nights sold on the portals against nights declared for the tourist tax. If they do not match, the problem predates 2026 and needs clearing up now.

Anyone also selling directly from their own website has an advantage here: the more weight the direct channel carries, the less you depend on the accuracy of listings you do not control.

Why there are no amounts in this article

You will have read precise figures elsewhere. We went looking for them too: the trade sources agree neither on the amounts nor on some of the dates they take effect, and on top of that part of the penalties and requirements are regional, so a figure that holds in Campania may not hold in Lombardy. Publishing a wrong number, in an article somebody will use to make a decision, is worse than not publishing one.

Where to check, with first-hand sources:
  • Ministry of Tourism — BDSR: the CIN application, the status of your file, the unit's registered details.
  • Normattiva for the text in force of art. 13-ter of decree-law 145/2023 and conversion law 191/2023.
  • EUR-Lex for the text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1028.
  • Your region's tourism portal for the regional code, local requirements and local penalties.
  • Your accountant for the tax side, which is not covered here.
If a figure does not come from one of these sources, treat it as an indication rather than as a fact.

The questions we are asked most

I run a hotel, not a short-term let: does this concern me?

The CIN applies to hotels as well, so yes for that part. The European Regulation is designed for short-term rentals intermediated by platforms: it concerns you to the extent that you sell through those channels.

If I only let through one platform, is there less to do?

The obligations are the same, but you have one point of exposure fewer — and one concentration risk more: if that listing is suspended over an inconsistent piece of data, the business stops altogether.

The platform transmits the data: do I still have to report my guests?

Yes. They are two distinct flows, with different legal bases and different recipients. Reporting guests to the police remains an obligation that falls on you.

Should I remove the CIN from my listings for privacy reasons?

No, quite the opposite: publishing it in the listings is part of the obligation. It identifies the property, it is not personal data to be protected.

Does anything change if I manage properties on behalf of others?

The amount of work changes, not the substance: every unit has its own code and its own data, and consistency has to be checked for each. This is the case where channel automation stops being convenient and becomes necessary.

In short

From 20 May 2026 the CIN is no longer a piece of paperwork to file away: it is the key by which listings, registers and activity data get compared. The work to be done is not understanding a complicated law — it is tidying up information you probably already have, scattered across different channels, written in different ways.

Half an hour of checking today is worth more than any amount of reading about penalties. And, as almost always in these cases, the tidying is worth doing anyway: a customer who finds the same address and the same details on every channel trusts you more, regardless of who else is comparing them.

We will tidy up your channels, once

An inventory of every live listing, your data aligned with the national database, ghost pages closed, and the code propagated from a single point. We do this for properties and property managers in Campania.

Let us talk about your case Message us on WhatsApp
